The World Wars, 1914–1945

Nine battles from the canal at Mons in 1914 to the Poles on Monte Cassino in 1944: the first British battle of the Great War, the Serbian stand at the Babuna pass, the Newfoundlanders on the first day of the Somme, the anti-tank guns at Snipe in the desert, the Rangers at Cisterna, three battles for Cassino and the Japanese counter-offensive on Bougainville. Every rule is in the Rules; this book holds the armies' figures for both wars, the wound tables their battles roll on, the battlefields, and a Newfoundland section followed across no man's land on 1 July 1916.

The battlefields: Mons 1914, The Babuna pass 1915, Beaumont-Hamel 1916, Snipe 1942, The Rangers at Cisterna 1944, Snakeshead Ridge and the abbey 1944, Hill 700 1944, Cassino town and Castle Hill 1944, The Poles at Point 593 and Phantom Ridge 1944.

The period's fighting

This book covers two wars: 1914 to 1918 and 1939 to 1945. Its battles run from the canal at Mons in August 1914 to the jungle of Bougainville in March 1944. In both, armies of millions fought, and most of the killing was done by guns the victims never saw.

Armies

In 1914 France, Germany, Russia and Austria-Hungary went to war with armies of conscripts, young men called up each year and kept on the reserve after their service. Britain had a small army of regulars, the BEF of 1914, raised by voluntary enlistment. Lord Kitchener asked for volunteers, and by January 1915, the UK Parliament's history records, over 1 million had come forward.

Many joined with their friends. In late August 1914 General Sir Henry Rawlinson appealed to the London stockbrokers, and they filled a battalion of the Royal Fusiliers in a week. A few days later Lord Derby called for "a battalion of pals" in Liverpool, and 1,500 men came in two days. These Pals went into action together, and were often cut down together: of an estimated 700 Accrington Pals at Serre on 1 July 1916, 235 were killed and 350 wounded.

Volunteering could not keep up with the losses. The Military Service Act of January 1916 made single men of 18 to 41 in Great Britain liable for service; a second act in May took in married men. Conscription was never applied in Ireland. It raised about 2.5 million men over the war.

The empires fought with colonial and Dominion troops. Over 1 million Indian soldiers served overseas, and the first Indian force reached Marseille on 30 September 1914. Marc Michel counts about 200,000 West Africans raised by France, of whom more than 135,000 fought in Europe and 30,000 were killed. Australia sent 416,809 men, the Australian War Memorial says, and twice voted down conscription. Newfoundland, Canada, New Zealand and South Africa sent their own.

In 1939 Britain did not wait. The National Service (Armed Forces) Act of 3 September 1939 made men of 18 to 41 liable at once. The United States began its first peacetime draft on 16 September 1940, and over 10 million men were inducted before it ended in 1947. Germany, the Soviet Union and Japan fought with conscripts. The Indian Army stayed volunteer: it grew from under 200,000 men in 1939 to over 2.5 million in 1945, the largest volunteer army in history. At Cassino in 1944 British, New Zealanders, Indians, Gurkhas, French and the 2nd Polish Corps all fought for the same mountain.

Arms

The infantryman of 1914 carried a bolt-action rifle. The British Short Magazine Lee-Enfield held 10 rounds, loaded 5 at a time from a charger, and a trained man could fire 20 to 30 aimed rounds in a minute. The Germans had the Mauser.

The machine gun, belt-fed and water-cooled, such as the British Vickers and the German MG 08, could be served by a small team from a pit. With barbed wire in front of it, it stopped most of the attacks of the war. But the great killer was artillery. Shell fragments caused about 60% of all wounds, the Imperial War Museum says. The gunners learned to fire a creeping barrage, a wall of shells that moved forward in steps, 50 to 100 yards every few minutes, with the infantry close behind. By September 1916 it was the standard British method.

Trench war brought back the grenade. The British adopted the Mills bomb as the No. 5 in 1915 and made over 33 million of them; its fuse burned for 7 seconds, cut to 4 after 1940. The trench mortar threw a bomb high, to drop into a trench. Stokes mortars were first used in battle at Loos on 25 September 1915.

On 22 April 1915, near Ypres, the Germans opened over 6,000 cylinders of chlorine against the French line. This was the first great gas attack. Phosgene followed in December 1915 and mustard gas, at Ypres, on 12 July 1917. Gas wounded far more men than it killed. In the American Expeditionary Forces it caused 70,522 casualties, nearly a third of the total; 1,221 of them died.

The tank first went into action at Flers-Courcelette on the Somme on 15 September 1916. Fourth Army had 49; many broke down before the start. By 4 July 1918, at Hamel, 60 tanks went in with the Australians, and carrier tanks brought up ammunition.

The sub-machine gun, a light automatic firing pistol rounds, came last. The German MP 18 reached units only in mid-1918. Many accounts arm the storm troops of the spring offensive with it, but there is no firm evidence that it reached the front so early. By 1939-45 sub-machine guns were common in every army. The Americans went further. The M1 Garand, a self-loading rifle with an 8-round clip, became their service rifle in 1936, and about 5.4 million were made in the war. The British kept the bolt action, in the No. 4 rifle adopted in 1941.

The anti-tank gun was the infantry's answer to the tank. The British 2-pounder gave way in 1942 to the 6-pounder, first used at Gazala that May, which could pierce any enemy tank then in service (see Snipe). Infantry also carried rocket launchers such as the American bazooka.

Aircraft joined the land battle. When the Germans crossed the Meuse in 1940, Stuka dive-bombers kept the French defenders under cover. In the desert the RAF began to put a controller with the forward troops, who called down fighter-bombers circling in a "cab rank", and the method was refined in Italy and Normandy.

Battles

On the Western Front each side dug a trench system: a front line, a support line 200 to 300 yards behind, a reserve line behind that, and communication trenches between them. In front lay belts of wire 15 metres deep or more. German dugouts went down 4 metres and more, some three storeys. Attacks failed for the same few reasons. The bombardment rarely cut all the wire or reached the men in the dugouts; the eight-day bombardment before the Somme did neither. When it lifted, the defenders came up and manned their machine guns. Where men did get in, their supplies and guns, drawn by horses, could not follow far beyond the railheads. From 1917 the Germans held their line in depth, with strongpoints spread over hundreds of metres.

The Germans looked for a way through. From December 1915 Captain Willy Rohr trained storm troops: small groups that worked forward under each other's fire, went round strongpoints and pushed on through the weak places. At Riga in September 1917 Georg Bruchmüller added a short, violent bombardment. In March 1918 the German 18th Army advanced more than 50 km in under a week, then outran its supplies and guns. The Allies' answer was the combined-arms attack. At Hamel on 4 July 1918 Lieutenant-General John Monash planned for 90 minutes and took his objectives in 93: infantry behind a creeping barrage, with tanks, and aircraft that dropped 112,000 rounds of ammunition to the forward troops.

In 1939-45 the war moved. Tanks, lorries and aircraft carried the mobile war through Poland and France and across Russia. In the desert of North Africa there was room to manoeuvre and little cover, and armies sowed mines: some 3 million were laid round El Alamein, and most were never cleared. In Italy the Allies fought up a narrow peninsula of mountains and rivers. The Gustav Line ran about 100 miles across it, with Monte Cassino at its heart. Few roads climbed the mountains; supplies went up by mule and on men's backs, and on the rock the infantry built stone sangars because they could not dig. In the jungle of the Pacific, as at Bougainville, men held pillbox lines behind belts cleared out of the jungle, and disease put more men in hospital than the enemy did.

Wounds and medicine

Shell wounds were the commonest: torn, irregular wounds, driven full of dirt. The farmland of the Western Front was rich in manure, and gas gangrene and tetanus followed.

The wounded went back by a chain of evacuation. Each British battalion had a medical officer and at least 16 stretcher-bearers. They carried a man to the Regimental Aid Post near the front; then to an Advanced Dressing Station, run by a Field Ambulance; then to a Casualty Clearing Station, a tented hospital, the nearest place to the front where women nurses served. Ambulance trains and barges took him on to the base hospitals, and hospital ships home.

A thigh bone broken by a bullet or shell fragment had killed most men who suffered it. The Thomas splint, devised by Hugh Owen Thomas and brought to the army by his nephew Robert Jones, held the leg straight and still. Introduced at the front in 1916, it cut deaths from fractured femurs from about 80% to about 20% by 1918.

Blood transfusion came to the front in 1917. In the spring Lawrence Bruce Robertson, a Canadian, set up transfusion at a casualty clearing station. Oswald Robertson, an American, kept blood in bottles with citrate and dextrose, on ice, for up to 26 days: the first blood bank. In 1939-45 the American Red Cross drew more than 13 million pints. The Americans began with dried plasma, but the British were saving more lives with whole blood, and by 1944 whole blood was being flown from the United States to Europe and the Pacific.

The sulpha drugs came first. American soldiers carried a field dressing coated with sulphanilamide, and medics shook sulpha powder into wounds. Penicillin was scarce in 1943, and every issue had to be approved, but by the landings in Normandy in June 1944 there was enough for the Allied wounded.

Men broke as well as bled. Soldiers in the winter of 1914-15 called it shell shock. Charles Myers, an army psychologist, urged that men be treated promptly, close to the front, and expected to recover; in 1939-45 the British and Americans adopted his methods and spoke of battle exhaustion. Trench foot, from standing for days in cold water, cost the British about 75,000 casualties and the Americans about 2,000, R. L. Atenstaedt finds. Whale oil, dry socks and men paired to check each other's feet had cut it greatly by the winter of 1917-18.

In the Pacific the enemy was malaria. In 1943 alone, G. Dennis Shanks writes, over 100,000 cases were reported among American troops in the South and Southwest Pacific, at rates of up to 250 per 1,000 men a year in the Solomons and New Guinea. Atabrine tablets kept it down; a division taken out of those islands was not fit to fight again for six months.

The women of Pervyse

Elsie Knocker, a trained nurse, and Mairi Chisholm, an 18-year-old who rode a motorcycle, came to Belgium in September 1914 with Dr Hector Munro's Flying Ambulance Corps. They decided they could save more men by treating them at the front than at the end of the long road back. In November they set up their own first-aid post in a cellar at Pervyse, close behind the Belgian trenches. Knocker treated the wounded; Chisholm drove them to hospital, often under fire. They raised their own money. King Albert gave them the Order of Leopold in 1915, and the British gave them the Military Medal in 1917. A gas shell caught them on 17 March 1918, and the post closed. Their book, The Cellar-House of Pervyse, came out in 1917.

The new faces of Sidcup

Harold Gillies, a New Zealand surgeon, saw the faces torn away by shell fragments in France in 1915. He began to rebuild them. He persuaded the army to open the Queen's Hospital at Sidcup, in Kent, for facial and jaw wounds; patients came from June 1917, and it opened officially on 16 August. Gillies and his team made the tubed pedicle: a flap of skin, rolled into a tube and left joined at both ends, swung from the chest or forehead to the face while it kept its own blood supply. Henry Tonks, a surgeon turned painter, drew the patients before and after. About 11,572 operations were done at Sidcup before it closed in 1925.

Women

Women served as nurses in both wars: in the army's own nursing services and, from Britain, as VADs of the Voluntary Aid Detachments. By 1918 the British Red Cross had over 90,000 VADs. They had to be between 23 and 38, and served at home and abroad. In 1939-45 over 59,000 women served in the US Army Nurse Corps.

Women also joined the armies as auxiliaries, so that men could be sent to the front. The Women's Army Auxiliary Corps, later Queen Mary's, began recruiting in March 1917; over 57,000 served, 17,000 of them overseas, as cooks, clerks and mechanics. The Auxiliary Territorial Service was formed on 9 September 1938. From December 1941 unmarried British women of 20 to 30 were called up, and by VE Day the ATS had over 190,000 members. From 1941 ATS women made up two-thirds of the mixed anti-aircraft batteries, working the instruments that aimed the guns.

In Russia in 1917 Maria Bochkareva raised a Women's Battalion, which went into action in the June Offensive. In 1941-45 over 800,000 women served in the Soviet forces, most of them as medics and nurses, but also as snipers, machine gunners, tank crew and pilots. The 588th Night Bomber Regiment, all women, flew over 30,000 sorties.

Lady Death

Lyudmila Pavlichenko was in her fourth year of history at Kyiv University. When Germany invaded in June 1941 she went to the recruiting office in Odessa, where they offered her nursing; she wanted the infantry. She became a sniper in the 25th Rifle Division and was credited with 187 kills in the siege of Odessa. She fought on at Sevastopol until June 1942, when mortar fragments struck her in the face. Her count then stood at 309, 36 of them snipers. In 1942 she toured the United States with Eleanor Roosevelt, the first Soviet citizen received at the White House. In Chicago she asked the crowd whether the men had not been "hiding behind my back for too long". She was made a Hero of the Soviet Union in 1943.

For the GM

Expect a world-war fight to be decided by fire, and most of it unseen. Shells and mortar bombs did most of the wounding, so a man in the open is in danger even when no enemy is in sight, and a man in a trench, a hole or a cellar is far safer. Wire and machine guns stop an attack in the open; a barrage, smoke, tanks or the dark get it across. In 1914-18 a wounded man's life depends on the stretcher-bearers and the chain behind them: the aid post, the dressing station, the casualty clearing station, the Thomas splint and, from 1917, blood. There are no antibiotics until sulpha in 1939-45 and penicillin in 1943-44. In the trenches and the jungle, cold water and mosquitoes will take as many men as the enemy.

What is switched on

Modern fire, in full: machine guns, barrages, trenches, digging in, and more men put down. Armour and mines, for the tanks, carriers and anti-tank guns at Snipe and the minefields of the desert. Air and night devices for aircraft from 1944 (the page leaves the date to the GM); night vision and landing by air belong to later wars. The wounded go back by motor ambulance, as the Rules' After the battle says. Wounds heal and fester as the Rules' Recovery says: it does not yet count the sulpha drugs of the Second World War or the penicillin of 1944.

Trouble at work

First World War (1914-1918)

d10 Trouble
1 An accident: hurt, and 1d6 days of work and pay lost.
2 Shellfire or a raid hits the workplace: a Dodge check, or a wound.
3 The Military Police check passes, and his papers must hold up.
4 Pay is stopped or docked for 'deductions'.
5 Gas, TNT or fumes: a Leechcraft check, or a week ill.
6 A comrade is caught pilfering and names him.
7 Recalled to the unit early: the term is cut short.
8 A quarrel with the locals over a woman, a debt or a fight.
9 Influenza sweeps the camp.
10 Suspected of spying: held and questioned for 1d3 days.

Second World War (1939-1945)

d10 Trouble
1 An industrial accident: 1d6 days of work lost.
2 An air raid or a torpedo: a Dodge check, or a wound.
3 Military police, Feldgendarmerie or Kempeitai check papers.
4 A black-market sting: the stake is lost, or he is arrested.
5 A strike or a layoff: the term ends on half pay.
6 An informer sells his name.
7 Recalled or drafted early.
8 A fight with a rival gang, crew or shift.
9 Illness (malaria, typhus, VD): a Leechcraft check.
10 The ship is sunk, the cell blown or the warehouse raided: a fight.

What each skill is for

First World War (1914-1918)

Skill Use Usually Against Success Failure Fumble
Persuade Haggle: Beat down a price. Ordinary the seller (Persuade) A tenth off (a quarter on a critical). The list price. No sale today.
Persuade Find a billet: Talk a village or a householder into a bed and a meal. Ordinary the householder or headman (Presence) Fed and bedded tonight: no keep to pay. He pays his keep, or sleeps rough. The village turns against the party: trouble.
Persuade Talk past a guard: Get by a sentry, a gate or the provost without the right papers. Hard the sentry or provost (Wits) Through. Turned back. Held as a deserter or a spy.
Persuade Question a prisoner: Get a prisoner or a local to talk. Ordinary the prisoner (Nerve) He tells what he knows (the GM decides how much is true). Nothing. He lies, and is believed.
Command Drive a hard task: Get men to do something hard and tiring: dig all night, march on after dark, cross a river. Ordinary — Done. Done slowly, or only half. They refuse.
Command Keep order: Stop plunder, drinking or a mutinous mood. Hard — They obey. Some slip away to it. They turn on him.
Letters Read or write: Read an order, a letter or a map's names; write a report. Easy — Read or written. Slowly, or with mistakes. He gets it wrong and does not know it.
Letters Forge a pass: Make a pass, an order or a billeting ticket that will be believed. Hard whoever checks it (Watch) It passes. Doubted: Talk past a guard instead. Seen through: held as a deserter or a spy.
Craft Mend kit: Mend a weapon, harness, boots, a cart or a radio set; a day's work. Ordinary — Mended. Not yet: another day. Ruined.
Craft Make something: Make ladders, a raft, a shelter, snowshoes or a litter from what is to hand. Ordinary — Made. Takes twice as long. It fails when it is used.
Fieldcraft Track: Follow men or animals. Ordinary the men being followed (Stealth) On their trail. Lost it. On the wrong trail.
Fieldcraft Find the way: Cross country without roads or a guide; at night, hard. Ordinary — On the way. Half a day lost. Lost: a day, or into the enemy.
Fieldcraft Hunt or gather: Find food or water for himself in the country. Ordinary — Fed today: no keep to pay. Nothing found. Something that makes him ill.
Watch Spot: See an ambush, a man hiding, a trap or a thing out of place. Ordinary whoever is hiding (Stealth) Seen. Missed. Sure there is nothing there.
Watch Search: Search a house, a body or a baggage wagon. Easy — Found what there is. Missed it. Missed it and left traces.
Stealth Sneak: Get past sentries, into a camp or away from one. Ordinary the sentries (Watch) Unseen. Seen, but not yet caught. Walks into them.
Stealth Steal: Lift a purse, a horse or rations unseen. Hard the owner or the guard (Watch) Taken. Not taken. Caught in the act: the provost.
Leechcraft Diagnose: Tell what a sick man has, and whether it will spread. Ordinary — Named: the GM tells which sickness. Unsure. Wrong.
Signals Get through: Raise another station, mend a line or a set, or send a message in code. Ordinary — Through. Not yet: try again next hour. The set or line is out until mended.
Strength Force or carry: Force a door, lift a beam, carry a wounded man. Ordinary — Done. Not alone. Strained: a step of fatigue.
Agility Climb or jump: Climb a wall, jump a ditch, keep his feet on ice. Ordinary — Over. Not this way. Falls: roll a fall as a wound.
Endurance Endure: Keep going: swim, go without sleep, hold out in the cold. Ordinary — Holds out. A step of fatigue. Collapses, or goes under.
Wits Notice or remember: Recall a face, a road or a password; work something out. Ordinary — Yes. No. Remembers it wrong.
Nerve Keep his head: Stay calm out of a fight: under shelling in a dugout, at a hanging, before an officer. Ordinary — Steady. Shaken: −10 to his next check. Breaks: runs, freezes or lashes out.
Presence Impress: Stare a man down, make a first impression, be remembered. Ordinary the other man (Presence) He gives way. No effect. Made an enemy.

Drive Drive under pressure: Drive off the road, at night without lights, or under fire. Ordinary — Through. Slowed or lost. Ditched or overturned.

Fieldcraft Find the way: Cross country without roads or a guide; at night, hard. Ordinary — On the way. Half a day lost. Lost: a day, or into the enemy.
Fieldcraft Hunt or gather: Find food or water for himself in the country. Ordinary — Fed today: no keep to pay. Nothing found. Something that makes him ill.
Watch Spot: See an ambush, a man hiding, a trap or a thing out of place. Ordinary whoever is hiding (Stealth) Seen. Missed. Sure there is nothing there.
Watch Search: Search a house, a body or a baggage wagon. Easy — Found what there is. Missed it. Missed it and left traces.
Stealth Sneak: Get past sentries, into a camp or away from one. Ordinary the sentries (Watch) Unseen. Seen, but not yet caught. Walks into them.
Stealth Steal: Lift a purse, a horse or rations unseen. Hard the owner or the guard (Watch) Taken. Not taken. Caught in the act: the provost.
Leechcraft Diagnose: Tell what a sick man has, and whether it will spread. Ordinary — Named: the GM tells which sickness. Unsure. Wrong.
Signals Get through: Raise another station, mend a line or a set, or send a message in code. Ordinary — Through. Not yet: try again next hour. The set or line is out until mended.
Strength Force or carry: Force a door, lift a beam, carry a wounded man. Ordinary — Done. Not alone. Strained: a step of fatigue.
Agility Climb or jump: Climb a wall, jump a ditch, keep his feet on ice. Ordinary — Over. Not this way. Falls: roll a fall as a wound.
Endurance Endure: Keep going: swim, go without sleep, hold out in the cold. Ordinary — Holds out. A step of fatigue. Collapses, or goes under.
Wits Notice or remember: Recall a face, a road or a password; work something out. Ordinary — Yes. No. Remembers it wrong.
Nerve Keep his head: Stay calm out of a fight: under shelling in a dugout, at a hanging, before an officer. Ordinary — Steady. Shaken: −10 to his next check. Breaks: runs, freezes or lashes out.
Presence Impress: Stare a man down, make a first impression, be remembered. Ordinary the other man (Presence) He gives way. No effect. Made an enemy.

Wound tables

Each battle rolls its wounds on a table built from the record of that war, and these are the notes on where each one comes from. The tables themselves are in the printed tables and the wound roller. A gameplay-adjusted table is re-weighted from bone evidence to stand for every blow that landed, not only the ones that marked bone; an evidence table is the record itself.

WWI 1914-18 - penetrating wounds

Primary penetrating wounds in WWI casualties.

How sure: taken directly from a source. Region totals are from the source. The split inside each region uses body exposure (design estimate). Extremities are split 40% arms / 60% legs, the average of the WWII, Korea and Vietnam hospital figures in Neel (1973) Table 7 (design estimate).

Rolled by: the battlefields of Mons 1914, The Babuna pass 1915, Beaumont-Hamel 1916; the armies of The British Empire, Newfoundland, France, Germany, The United States (1917-1918), Russian, Serbian, Austro-Hungarian, Bulgarian.

Sources:

  • Borden Institute, Weapons Effects and War Wounds, ch. 1, Table 1-2: anatomical distribution of primary penetrating wounds (%): head/neck/face 17, thorax 4, abdomen 2, extremity 70, other 7.

WWII Italy 1944 - killed in action

Wounds on 983 American soldiers killed by missiles (bullets and shell fragments), examined in Italian military cemeteries, 1944. 7,006 wounds.

How sure: taken directly from a source. Region totals are from the source. The split inside each region uses body exposure (design estimate).

Rolled by: no battle here: it is the evidence the others are built from.

Sources:

  • US Army Medical Department, Wound Ballistics in World War II, ch. 6, Table 118: lower extremities 29.7%, thorax 25.7%, upper extremities 20.8%, head 8.8%, abdomen 6.4%, buttocks 4.9%, neck 3.7%, genitalia 0.3%.

Bougainville 1944 - wounded

US soldiers wounded by Japanese rifle, machine-gun, mortar, grenade and artillery fire, Bougainville, 1944 (1,162 single-region wounds).

How sure: taken directly from a source. Region counts are from the source. The split inside each region uses body exposure (design estimate).

Rolled by: no battle here: it is the evidence the others are built from.

Sources:

  • Oughterson et al., Wound Ballistics study of the Bougainville campaign (US Army Medical Department, 1944; NLM scan nlmuid-46921110R): living wounded by region - head, face, neck 240; chest 144; abdomen 66; upper extremities 319; lower extremities 393. Excludes 332 multi-region wounds and 547 minor wounds returned to duty.

Battlefields

Each battlefield lays out on the field map under Battlefield. What follows is what the field and its phases hold, and, briefly, what happened there.

Mons, 23 August 1914 (the Nimy salient)

  • The armies: British and Germans.
  • Fought for: the railway bridge at Nimy, attacked by the Germans.
  • The field: 150 by 120 hexes of 10 m, about 1,500 by 1,040 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Overcast, calm or light air from the south-west.
  • Wounds: WWI 1914-18 - penetrating wounds.
  • On the travel map: Mons, 1914 (Condé to Binche), at Nimy bridges.

The campaign

Britain declared war on Germany on 4 August 1914. The British Expeditionary Force (BEF), about 80,000 men in two corps and a cavalry division, began to cross to France on 9 August and marched into Belgium on the left of the French Fifth Army. The German First Army was coming through Belgium on the right wing of the German advance.

On 21 August Private John Parr of the 4th Middlesex was killed on patrol, the first British soldier to die in the war. On 22 August the BEF reached Mons. II Corps under General Sir Horace Smith-Dorrien took the line of the Mons-Condé canal west and north of the town. I Corps stood back on the right, at an angle to it.

North of Mons the canal bends north in a loop round the village of Nimy. Doyle calls it "a most awkward loop": troops in it could be shelled from both sides. The 3rd Division held it: the 4th Royal Fusiliers of the 9th Brigade the western face and the bridges at Nimy, the 4th Middlesex of the 8th Brigade the eastern face as far as Obourg.

The times below are British. The BEF kept Greenwich time in 1914 and German clocks ran an hour ahead; the official historian, Edmonds, converts German times to British.

The places

  • The Mons-Condé canal: about 60 feet wide and 7 feet deep, Kendall says, with 18 bridges on this stretch.
  • Nimy: the village inside the loop of the canal, about 2 miles north of the centre of Mons.
  • The Nimy railway bridge: on the Paris-Brussels line, where Dease's two machine guns stood.
  • The Nimy road bridge: a swing bridge on the Chaussée de Bruxelles, the road north out of Mons.
  • Lock No. 6 and the park gate bridge: further west, held by Captain Byng's company of the Fusiliers.
  • Obourg: the station and bridge on the eastern face of the salient, held by the 4th Middlesex.
  • The Grand Place, Mons: where the Fusiliers rested on 22 August, and fell back to on 23 August.
  • St Symphorien: east of Mons. Dease, and the German soldier Oskar Niemeyer, are buried in the military cemetery there.

The leaders

  • Sir John French (British, commander of the BEF).
  • Sir Horace Smith-Dorrien (British, II Corps): held the canal with the 3rd and 5th Divisions.
  • Hubert Hamilton (British, 3rd Division): killed at La Couture on 14 October.
  • Norman McMahon (British, 4th Royal Fusiliers): lieutenant colonel. At the School of Musketry he had introduced the standard of 15 aimed rounds a minute. Killed near Hooge on 11 November.
  • Charles Hull (British, 4th Middlesex): lieutenant colonel, at Obourg and through the retreat.
  • Maurice Dease (British, 4th Royal Fusiliers): lieutenant, the battalion's machine-gun officer, aged 24.
  • Alexander von Kluck (German, First Army).
  • Ferdinand von Quast (German, IX Corps): his 18th Division attacked the salient; its 35th Brigade had Infantry Regiment No. 84 and Fusilier Regiment No. 86.

The battle

German guns opened on the salient at dawn. Ernest Hamilton, writing in 1916, has the first infantry attack at 08:00 on the north-west corner of the loop. About 09:00 four German battalions, of the 84th Regiment by the visitmons guide, came at the Nimy bridges in close column. Rifle and machine-gun fire at short range brought the leading sections down together. The survivors took cover, and about half an hour later came on again in extended order.

At the railway bridge Captain Ashburner's company held the line with Dease's two guns. Dease was hit below the knee early on, and again as he went between the guns. Captain Forster, beside Ashburner, was shot through the arm and stomach. Ashburner was wounded in the head. Second Lieutenant Mead brought up a platoon. He was hit in the head, had the wound dressed, went back to the line and was killed. Captain Bowden-Smith and Lieutenant Smith brought up another, and both were badly wounded within ten minutes.

The visitmons guide says the Germans attacked in force at 11:00 and brought up more guns. At Obourg the 4th Middlesex, under fire from about 08:00, asked for help around midday, and two companies of the 2nd Royal Irish came up from Hyon. On the German side Musketier Oskar Niemeyer of the 84th swam the canal under fire, came back with a boat, and worked the swing bridge so that his comrades could cross. He was killed.

The order to retire came at 13:10, by the visitmons guide, and the Fusiliers went at 13:40. By then most of the machine-gun crews were down. Dease had been hit a fifth time and could not move. Lieutenant Steele carried him back, and he died of his wounds. Private Sidney Godley took over a gun and kept it firing while the battalion withdrew across about 250 yards of open ground. The Fusiliers fell back along the Chaussée de Bruxelles into Mons, leaving most of their wounded in German hands. The official report gave their loss as 7 officers and 105 other ranks; Ernest Hamilton says the Middlesex lost 15 officers and 353 men.

The Germans crossed that afternoon and took Nimy. They burned 108 houses along the Chaussée, killed 22 civilians, and drove hostages, among them the mayor, ahead of them into Mons. At 02:00 on 24 August II Corps was ordered to retreat. The retreat went on into September, more than 250 miles, through Le Cateau on 26 August to the Marne.

Where the accounts disagree

  • When it began. Ernest Hamilton has a first attack at 08:00 and the attack on the Nimy bridge about 09:00; Kendall, attacks at 08:00 and 09:00; the visitmons guide, the 84th advancing from 08:30; Wikipedia, the first assault at 09:00.
  • When the Fusiliers left. The visitmons guide has the order at 13:10 and the move at 13:40. Kendall says the order came at 14:00. Ernest Hamilton says the 3rd Division's brigades were ordered back at 15:00, as does Wikipedia.
  • Who held the road bridge. The visitmons guide puts Ashburner's company on both the road and railway bridges, with Byng's company further west at Lock No. 6. Kendall and Luscombe put Captain Forster with two platoons at the road bridge. Ernest Hamilton puts Byng's company on the Ghlin bridge, and Godley's VC there too.
  • The attackers. Ernest Hamilton counts four battalions in the first charge. Kendall gives six battalions of the 18th Division, about 6,000 men (he calls it III Corps; the Wikipedia articles and the German order of battle give IX Corps).
  • Dease's wounds and death. His citation says he was hit five times; O'Neill's regimental history, as Wikipedia gives it, makes the third wound fatal. Steele wrote to the family that he was first hit about 09:00. Ashcroft says he died about 15:30; the visitmons guide says in the ambulance, Wikipedia at the battalion aid post.
  • Godley's stand. Wikipedia says he threw the gun's parts into the canal and was taken there. Kendall and Ashcroft say two Belgians helped him to hospital in Mons, where the Germans found him. O'Neill says both guns were riddled with bullets before the end.
  • The losses. Edmonds gives the BEF's loss at Mons as just over 1,600. For the Germans, Zuber argues from regimental histories for no more than 2,000; Keegan and Herwig give about 5,000. The German medical history counts 2,145 dead and missing and 4,932 wounded for the whole First Army, 20-31 August.

Two hours on the bridge

Sidney Godley was a private in the 4th Royal Fusiliers' machine-gun section at the Nimy railway bridge. When Dease was hit for the last time, Lieutenant Steele asked for a man to stay on the gun and cover the battalion's withdrawal. Godley took it. A shell burst put a fragment into his back and a bullet hit him in the head. His citation speaks of "fighting his machine gun under a hot fire for two hours" after he was wounded. When the ammunition ran out he broke up the gun and threw the pieces into the canal. He was taken prisoner, and spent the war in a camp near Berlin, where he heard of his Victoria Cross. The King gave it to him on 15 February 1919.

How the field is drawn

The canal salient at Nimy, north of Mons, 23 August 1914, at 10 m a hex: 150 x 120 hexes, about 1500 m east to west and 1040 m north to south, north at the top: the canal loop across the middle, its two bridges near the tip, Nimy on the south bank, open fields and woods to the north. The canal, the village, the woods and the bridges are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is mid-morning, in our own words, with round numbers for play. Water (the canal) can be crossed only at the bridges.

The phases

From exchange Phase What happens
1 The first assault 09:00: IR 84 comes at the bridges of the salient in close order.
31 A renewed attack Half an hour after the first is beaten off, a wider attack comes in through the woods (which battalion is our reading).
121 The attack in force 11:00: the Germans attack in force (that the supporting battalion went in then is our reading).
251 Withdrawal 13:10: the Fusiliers are ordered back; they go at 13:40.

The accounts to choose

Where the sources disagree on something the battle turns on, the field map asks which account to fight (or rolls it, each as likely). The first is the game's own, and the enemy commander's benchmark is run on it; a battle on another is scored against history only.

Question The accounts
How many Germans attacked? Four battalions (the game's reading; Ernest Hamilton counts four in the first charge) (the game's own); Six battalions, about 6,000 (Kendall)
When were the Fusiliers ordered back? 13:10 (the visitmons guide) (the game's own); 14:00 (Kendall); 15:00 (Ernest Hamilton and Wikipedia, for the 3rd Division's brigades)

The Babuna pass, November 1915

  • The armies: Serbians and Bulgarians.
  • Fought for: the saddle of the Babuna pass, attacked by the Bulgarians.
  • The field: 130 by 110 hexes of 10 m, about 1,300 by 950 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Overcast, breeze from the north.
  • Wounds: WWI 1914-18 - penetrating wounds.
  • On the travel map: Serbia, 1915 (the great retreat), at Babuna pass.
  • The record: the fight lasted about 931 exchanges (a minute each).

The campaign

On 6 October 1915 the German Eleventh Army and the Austro-Hungarian Third Army, under August von Mackensen, attacked Serbia across the Sava and the Danube. Belgrade fell on 9 October. Bulgaria joined the Central Powers, attacked across the border from 11 October and declared war on 14 October. Its First Army struck west towards Niš. Its Second Army, under Georgi Todorov, went into Macedonia to cut the railway from Niš to Salonika. It cut the line on 16 October and entered Skopje and Veles on 22 or 23 October.

A French and British force had begun to land at Salonika on 5 October. The French went up the Vardar to Krivolak, hoping to join hands with the Serbs. Between them and the Bulgarians at Veles stood a small Serbian force on the Babuna pass. The pass carried the road from Veles to Prilep, and so to Monastir (Bitola). While the Serbs held it, the road south to Monastir, and the hope of supplies from the south, stayed open.

The Nelson history says about 5,000 Serbs held the heights above the northern approach. In the first days of November they beat off a Bulgarian division and drove it back to Izvor, about a dozen miles from Veles. But that was only an advanced guard. Todorov's main force came down from the Veles front, and the Serbs were pushed back to the crest. They held it, Nelson says, for a week and more. A French column took the Vozartzi bridge on the Crna (the Tcherna) on 5 November and tried to climb the heights towards them, but it was beaten back.

The places

  • The Babuna pass: the saddle where the road from Veles to Prilep crosses the Babuna mountains.
  • Izvor: the village at the northern foot of the pass, about a dozen miles from Veles, where the Bulgarians were first driven back.
  • Veles: the town on the Vardar, in Bulgarian hands from late October, from which the main attack came.
  • Prilep: the town south of the pass, where Flora Sandes worked in the military hospital. The Bulgarians occupied it on 17 November.
  • Bitola (Monastir; Sandes's "Bitol"): the town further south, which gave the Serbian division its name, and the next stage of the retreat.
  • Skopje (Uskub): taken by the Bulgarians in late October, with Veles.
  • Krivolak and the Crna: where the French held a bridgehead on the Vardar and tried to reach the Serbs.
  • Salonika: the Greek port where the Allies landed, and where Sandes came ashore on 3 November.

The leaders

  • Radomir Putnik (Serbian, commander of the army): the stand at Babuna, Nelson says, bought him time to bring the main army away.
  • Colonel Wasitch (Serbian, Bitol Division): so Sandes calls him; the Wikipedia article on Sandes names him General Miloš Vasić. He let her stay with the regiment through the retreat and later enrolled her as a soldier.
  • Colonel Militch (Serbian, 2nd Regiment): the regiment's commandant, whose ambulance Sandes joined.
  • Flora Sandes (British, with the Serbian 2nd Regiment): a nurse aged 39, attached to the 2nd Regiment's ambulance near Babuna.
  • August von Mackensen (German, commander of the invasion).
  • Georgi Todorov (Bulgarian, Second Army): Nelson spells him Teodorov.
  • Maurice Sarrail (French, at Salonika): reached Salonika on 12 October and pushed the French up the Vardar.

The battle

The sources give no day-by-day account of the fighting at Babuna. Nelson gives the outline: a first Bulgarian attack beaten back to Izvor in the first days of November, then the main force from Veles, the Serbs pressed back to the crest, and the crest held for a week and more. Nelson says the Serbs faced in the end "the better part of six divisions". Sandes says they were outnumbered more than four to one.

Sandes explains why so few could hold so long, and why they could not hold longer. The position was strong, she writes, almost impregnable. But the commandant had an enormous front to hold with two regiments, and since the Bulgarians could walk round the lines, every available man was already in the firing line: there were no reserves. The Bulgarians had big guns. The Serbs had a few small cannon about ten years old. With a few big guns, she thought, they could have held the pass for any length of time.

Sandes reached the 2nd Regiment's ambulance about the middle of November, after a week at the military hospital in Prilep, which was full of men with dysentery lying on the floor. The ambulance was in tents by the road near Babuna. The next morning a battle was going on at Babuna, and the wounded came in all day. The path down the mountain was so steep that a badly wounded man could hardly be carried on a stretcher, so most of those who came in had walked down. Men who could not walk were sent on to the base hospital in ox wagons. They came in faster than the wagons could take them away.

A day or two later, at ten o'clock at night by Sandes's clock, the regiment was ordered to retreat from Babuna. The ambulance packed up in the wind and rain and went down the road for about eight hours. It passed through Prilep in the night and was between Prilep and Bitola at sunrise. Her dates put this in the middle of November, just before the Bulgarians entered Prilep on 17 November. The French could not now reach the Serbs, and fell back. On 25 November the Serbian government and high command decided to take the army across the mountains of Albania to the Adriatic. The 2nd Regiment went back by Bitola, fighting rearguard actions, Sandes says, for the next six weeks.

Where the accounts disagree

  • How many attacked. Nelson says the Serbs faced the better part of six divisions. Sandes says they were outnumbered more than four to one. Which Bulgarian division made the first attack, and which units came from Veles, is not given by either.
  • How many defended. Nelson gives about 5,000 Serbs. Sandes gives no number, but names the 2nd and 14th Regiments.
  • The height. Nelson calls the pass "a little over 2,000 feet high". A modern cycling survey puts the road summit at 1,090 m, about 3,600 feet.
  • The dates. Nelson puts the first Bulgarian repulse in the first days of November and the end of the stand a week and more after that, but gives no date for the end. Sandes's diary dates only her arrival at Salonika (3 November) and one evening in Prilep ("Monday, 8th"). The Wikipedia article on Prilep gives 17 November for its occupation.
  • Skopje and Veles. The Wikipedia article on the campaign has the Bulgarians reach Skopje on 22 October; the article on the Kosovo offensive, citing Hall, has them enter Skopje and Veles on 23 October.
  • The commander. Sandes calls the commandant of the Bitol Division Colonel Wasitch; the Wikipedia article on her calls him General Miloš Vasić.

Sixteen wounded in the tent

On the night the order came to leave Babuna, Flora Sandes had sixteen wounded men in the ambulance tent, twelve of whom could not walk. The order came at ten o'clock. The tent was struck in the wind and rain, and the wounded were lifted into ox wagons, four lying down in each. One man had a shrapnel wound in the ankle. Sandes dressed it by the light of a torch outside the tent while it was being taken down round her. Then the column set off down the road to Prilep in the dark. The wagons were on the road for about eight hours. They went through Prilep in the night, and the sun came up on them on the road to Bitola.

How the field is drawn

The Babuna pass on the road from Veles to Prilep, mid-November 1915, at 10 m a hex: 130 x 110 hexes, about 1300 m east to west and 950 m north to south, north at the top: the road climbs in hairpins from Izvor to the saddle in the middle, between two spurs that push north; the Serbian trenches run along the crest; the road goes on down towards Prilep at the bottom. The saddle, the spurs, the hairpins and the woods are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the day, the companies and the Bulgarian battalions are our reading, with round numbers for play. Machine guns and the Bulgarian divisions engaged are not in the sources found.

The phases

From exchange Phase What happens
1 The bombardment and the first attack Dawn, about 06:30: the Bulgarian guns open on the crest and a battalion comes up the road from Izvor.
61 Up the spurs About 07:30: a second battalion climbs the west spur into the fire from the trenches.
391 The flank pressed About 13:00: the Bulgarians press the east spur (which flank is our reading).
571 Reinforcements from Veles About 16:00: a fresh battalion comes up from the Veles front.
631 Dusk About 17:00: the light goes; the Serbs hang on along the crest.

Beaumont-Hamel, 1 July 1916 (the Newfoundland Park)

  • The armies: British and Germans.
  • Fought for: the German front line at Y Ravine, attacked by the British.
  • The field: 80 by 116 hexes of 10 m, about 800 by 1,000 m, east at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, calm or light air from the west.
  • Wounds: WWI 1914-18 - penetrating wounds.
  • On the travel map: Beaumont-Hamel, 1916 (Doullens to Bapaume), at Newfoundland Park (the battlefield).
  • The record: the fight lasted about 221 exchanges (a minute each).

The campaign

In 1916 the British and French planned an offensive on the Somme, to open on 1 July along a front of about 40 km. The northern flank of the British Fourth Army was VIII Corps under Lieutenant General Aylmer Hunter-Weston. Opposite Beaumont-Hamel stood his 29th Division, back from Gallipoli.

The Newfoundland Regiment, one battalion from the dominion of Newfoundland, had served at Gallipoli from September 1915 to January 1916. It reached France in March in the 88th Brigade. It was made the Royal Newfoundland Regiment only in 1917. Facing the division was Reserve Infantry Regiment 119 of the 26th (Württemberg) Reserve Division, which had held the sector for about 20 months. It had dug deep dugouts, and in Y Ravine shelters for a battalion.

The bombardment began on 24 June. The attack was put back from 29 June to 1 July, partly for the weather and partly to give the guns longer. The German wire survived in many places, and the men in the dugouts were largely unhurt. On the night of 30 June the Newfoundlanders marched up from Louvencourt to St John's Road, a support trench behind the front line.

The places

  • St John's Road: the support trench, out of German sight, from which the Newfoundlanders went over.
  • The British front line: on the crest about 250 m ahead, with bridges over the trench and lanes cut in the wire.
  • No man's land: open grass falling to the German wire, about 400 m wide opposite Y Ravine and narrower to the north-west.
  • The Danger Tree: a stripped tree about halfway across. A replica stands on the spot.
  • Y Ravine: a gully that forked at the German front line and ran back into the German position, its dugouts hidden in its sides.
  • Station Road: the road to the railway station in the valley behind the German line, the Newfoundlanders' objective.
  • Hawthorn Ridge: to the north, where a mine blew up the German redoubt ten minutes before zero. Its crater is still there.
  • The Newfoundland Memorial Park: about 74 acres bought by Newfoundland in 1921, the trenches left in place under a bronze caribou. The game's field is the middle of the park, from St John's Road to the German support trench, with Y Ravine on the left; the Hawthorn crater is off the board to the north.

The leaders

  • Aylmer Hunter-Weston (British, VIII Corps): wanted the Hawthorn mine fired early; it went at ten minutes before zero.
  • Henry de Beauvoir de Lisle (British, 29th Division): sent in two reserve battalions at 08:45.
  • Douglas Edward Cayley (British, 88th Brigade): ordered the Newfoundlanders forward "as soon as possible".
  • Arthur Lovell Hadow (British, 1st Newfoundland Regiment): finding the communication trenches choked, he sent the battalion over the open.
  • R. C. Pierce (British, 1st Royal Inniskilling Fusiliers): killed in the first wave.
  • Ellis (British, 1st Border): wounded in the second wave and brought in by Private Newcombe.
  • G. E. Malcolm (British, captain, 1st KOSB): tried to carry the attack on with about 40 men and was wounded.
  • Reserve Infantry Regiment 119 (German, the defenders): no source read for this page names its commander.

The battle

Times here are British, GMT+1; German clocks were an hour ahead. At 07:20 the Hawthorn Ridge mine went up, and RIR 119 came up from its dugouts. At 07:30 the barrage lifted, moving back 100 yards every two minutes, and the 86th and 87th Brigades went over. On the 87th's front the 2nd South Wales Borderers and 1st Royal Inniskilling Fusiliers led. The Border diary says the Borderers were cut down while still in their own wire. At about 07:35 the 1st KOSB and 1st Border crossed the bridges over their own front trench, ranged by the German gunners the day before, and were stopped in no man's land. Veterans Affairs says only parts of the Inniskillings, on the right, got into the German trenches.

White German signal rockets were taken for British success flares. At 08:45 de Lisle ordered the 1st Newfoundland Regiment and 1st Essex to take the German first trench and clear forward to Station Road. The trenches were full of wounded, so Hadow sent the Newfoundlanders over the top. The Essex, in view from Thiepval, had to use the trenches.

The Newfoundlanders left at 09:15, A and B Companies in front and C and D 100 yards behind. They went alone. Many were hit before they reached their own front line, and the war diary says the heaviest losses came in the gaps in the British wire, where men were "mown down in heaps". The survivors went on down the slope; most who reached the Danger Tree went no further, though the diary believed a few got close enough to throw bombs. Within 15 to 20 minutes most of the battalion was down. At 09:45 Hadow reported to brigade that the attack had failed.

The Essex reached the front line at 10:50 and attacked. A halt order from division had not reached them. Their two leading companies lost about 250 men before Lieutenant Colonel Halahan stopped them. At 14:00 the 88th Brigade took over the line from the 87th.

The 88th Brigade's diary put most losses down to machine guns; at the Danger Tree shrapnel hit many. Few wounded could crawl in before dark. Many died where they lay or were hit again, and some were not brought in for four nights. The tin triangles on their backs, meant to show the infantry to aircraft and gunners, flashed in the sun when a wounded man moved. Private Thomas White McGrath, a stretcher-bearer, brought in wounded in daylight under fire and won the Military Medal. Tony Turco counts 471 Newfoundland wounded evacuated, of whom 33 died of their wounds.

Where the accounts disagree

  • How many went forward. Veterans Affairs Canada, after Nicholson, gives 22 officers and 758 other ranks, about 780; elsewhere it says about 800. The National Archives blog says about 720. All agree that 68 answered the roll call.
  • The losses. The war diary of 7 July gives 684: 14 officers and 296 men killed, died of wounds or missing, and 12 officers and 362 men wounded. The Rooms gives 710: 233 dead, 91 missing and 386 wounded, as does The Canadian Encyclopedia (324 dead or missing, 386 wounded). Nicholson has all the officers and just under 658 men hit. The Commonwealth War Graves Commission records 243 deaths on 1 July (National Archives blog). Wikipedia puts the loss second only to the 10th West Yorkshires' 733 at Fricourt.
  • When the Essex went. The Essex war diary, Veterans Affairs and the Basildon Heritage Society say 10:50. The Royal Newfoundland Regiment Museum gives 09:55; the game follows the war diary.
  • Why the Essex were late. Veterans Affairs says they were in view from Thiepval and had to use the trenches. The Rooms says their commanding officer chose the trenches to spare his men.
  • When Hadow reported. The war diary and most accounts say 09:45. Turco gives 10:00.
  • The Inniskillings. Veterans Affairs says parts of the battalion got into the German first to third lines. Their war diary says they could not pass the German wire.
  • The mine. Wikipedia gives 40,000 lb of ammonal; the Imperial War Museum's caption 45,000 lb; Veterans Affairs and The Rooms 18,500 kg. The crater was 130 feet across and 58 deep by the museum, 40 m by 18 m by Heritage NL.
  • The distances. Veterans Affairs says more than 200 m to the British front line and more than 500 m on to the German trenches. Heritage NL puts the lines about 400 m apart opposite Y Ravine.
  • The German loss. Wikipedia, after the German sources, gives RIR 119's loss as 292 men for the whole day. The 29th Division lost 5,240.

Fifteen hours in no man's land

Private James McGrath was hit in the first rush on 1 July and hit again in the leg as he lay out. He later told the Newfoundland Quarterly that he lay in no man's land for fifteen hours. Then he crawled what he reckoned was a mile and a quarter back to the British line, only to find it empty, with the British guns firing heavily. The German reply kept him in a shell hole for another hour. Nearing a trench he was hit again, round the hip. Captain Windeler rescued him and carried him on his back two miles to a dressing station. "Thank God my wounds are all flesh wounds," McGrath wrote. Heritage NL puts his time out at about 17 hours.

How the field is drawn

Beaumont-Hamel, 1 July 1916, at 10 m a hex: 80 x 116 hexes, about 800 m north to south and 1000 m east to west, east at the top: St John's Road across the bottom, the British front line on the crest, the British wire and its few lanes, no man's land falling to the German wire and the German front system across the middle, Y Ravine running up from it on the left (north), the Danger Tree halfway across. The lines, the slope and the ravine are drawn to the distances the sources give, not traced from a trench map; the narrowing of no man's land to the north-west is off this board. RIR 119's companies and machine guns here are not known: those, and the British battalions' strengths (but the Inniskillings' 952 and the Newfoundlanders' 780), are ours, with round numbers. The British barrage lifted at zero and is not on call; the German field guns are. The Germans wear no steel helmets (whether RIR 119 had them on 1 July is not known); the British wear the Brodie. The German ammunition is in the dugouts (supply dumps); no man's land plays as open ground, falling only in the account (a slope hex would hide the forward slope from the German line).

The phases

From exchange Phase What happens

The accounts to choose

Where the sources disagree on something the battle turns on, the field map asks which account to fight (or rolls it, each as likely). The first is the game's own, and the enemy commander's benchmark is run on it; a battle on another is scored against history only.

Snipe, 27 October 1942 (El Alamein)

  • The armies: British and Germans and Italians.
  • Fought for: Snipe, attacked by the Germans and Italians.
  • The field: 200 by 160 hexes of 10 m, about 2,000 by 1,390 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, calm or light air from the north-west, dusk.
  • Wounds: WWII 1941-45 - hospitalized (Owens comparison set).
  • On the travel map: Snipe, 1942 (the coast to Miteiriya), at Snipe (the battlefield).
  • The record: the fight lasted about 806 exchanges (a minute each).

The campaign

Rommel's German and Italian army beat the British at Gazala in June 1942 and followed them into Egypt. It was stopped at El Alamein in July and at Alam Halfa in August. The line there ran about 40 miles from the sea to the Qattara Depression, so any attack had to go in from the front.

Montgomery's Eighth Army attacked on the night of 23 October 1942 (Operation Lightfoot). The infantry broke into the minefields, but the lanes were not cleared in time and the tanks could not get through. Rommel, away sick, came back on 25 October; his stand-in, Stumme, had died on the 24th. The tanks of both sides fought round the Kidney feature for three days.

On 26 October the 7th Motor Brigade, of the 1st Armoured Division, was ordered to push two battalions west at 23:00 onto two points, "Woodcock" and "Snipe", for the armoured brigades to pass through in the morning. The 2nd King's Royal Rifle Corps went for Woodcock. The 2nd Battalion The Rifle Brigade, under Lieutenant-Colonel Victor Buller Turner, went for Snipe. With Turner went his own six-pounders, two troops of 239 Battery, 76th (Royal Welch Fusiliers) Anti-Tank Regiment RA, and 16 sappers of the 7th Field Squadron RE. With 76 riflemen and 22 carriers the force came to about 300 men.

The places

  • El Alamein: the railway halt on the coast that gave the battle its name.
  • The Kidney feature: a kidney-shaped contour west of the British gaps, fought over from 24 October.
  • Snipe: the objective, about 1.5 miles south-west of the Kidney.
  • The Snipe hollow: a shallow oval depression, about 1,000 by 500 yards, with camelthorn and soft sand, where the battalion dug in short of the objective.
  • Woodcock: the 2nd KRRC's objective, north of Snipe; the battalion fell short of it.
  • The eastern ridge: the low rise behind the outpost, where the battalion's ambulances and lorries waited.
  • The western ridge: the low rise in front, over which the Italian tanks came.

The leaders

  • Victor Buller Turner (British, 2nd Rifle Brigade): 42, the brother of a First World War VC. He was wounded in the head and went on.
  • Tom Bird (British, S Company): commanded the battalion's anti-tank company, and drove ammunition round the guns in a jeep.
  • Charles Calistan (British, sergeant): his six-pounder held the south-west side at midday.
  • Ralph Noyes (British, artillery observer): went out to reconnoitre at 04:00 and did not come back, so the outpost had no guns on call.
  • Raymond Briggs (British, 1st Armoured Division): decided not to send his tanks forward to save the outpost.
  • T. J. B. Bosvile (British, 7th Motor Brigade): arranged the relief and the withdrawal.
  • Erwin Rommel (German, commander): ordered the counter-attack of 27 October.
  • Gustav von Vaerst (German, 15th Panzer Division): its tanks lay north of the outpost.
  • Stiffelmayer (German, battle group): his Gruppe of about 35 tanks and self-propelled guns had leaguered close to the hollow. The sources give no first name or rank.
  • Capitano Preve (Italian, Littorio): led 13 tanks of the Littorio's tank regiment against the west side.

The battle

The barrage came down at 22:55 on 26 October. Turner followed it on a bearing of 270 degrees rather than his navigator's 233, and the battalion set off at 23:10. At about 00:15 on 27 October, 4,000 yards out, it reached a hollow it took for Snipe, some 800 or 900 yards short. The carriers took prisoners and shot up three lorries at a leaguer close by. By 03:45 19 of the 27 six-pounders were dug in: 13 of the battalion's and 6 of the battery's.

At first light the tanks of 15th Panzer and the Littorio left their leaguers and moved off past the hollow, side-on to the guns. A Panzer IV Special was hit at about 30 yards. At 07:30 the 47th and 41st Royal Tank Regiments came over the eastern ridge, took Snipe for an enemy position and fired on it. They then lost heavily, and by 09:00 were pulled back, 47 RTR down to five Shermans and six Crusaders. The outpost was on its own.

At about 10:00 the carriers drove off Italian infantry massing to the west. By noon six carriers had been hit and set on fire, and ammunition was short. Preve's 13 tanks came over the western ridge; four were knocked out and the rest drew off. At about 13:00 eight more tanks and a self-propelled gun came in from the south-west, where only Calistan's gun was left. Turner and Lieutenant Jack Toms joined him, and the attack was stopped.

At about 16:00 British guns firing from the east hit the outpost again. At about 17:00 some 40 German and Italian tanks passed across the front of 239 Battery and S Company and lost heavily. A second wave of 15 Panzer IIIs turned on the north-west side, where only three guns could fire, with about 10 rounds each. It too was stopped. Dusk ended the attacks. The last anti-tank round was fired at 19:40.

Three carriers took the worst wounded back over the eastern ridge in the morning; of three more sent later, one was knocked out. The ambulances could not come forward through the fire. That night the 5th Royal Sussex, of the 133rd Lorried Infantry Brigade, came up to relieve the battalion, but dug in about 1,000 yards to the south-east and was not found. The survivors came out on foot late that night, the wounded on six carriers and three jeeps, with one gun. The other guns were left without their sights and breech blocks, and the dead were left behind.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The clock. Wikipedia, after Playfair, gives the start of Lightfoot in Egyptian Summer Time (GMT+3). Egypt put its clocks back to GMT+2 at midnight on 26/27 October 1942, and no account of Snipe says which clock it used. The game keeps GMT+3, on which the sun rose about 07:16 and set about 18:23 (our reckoning).
  • The guns. Wikipedia, after Latimer, gives 19 guns dug in of 27. Miskimon has the battalion bring 16 and the battery 11.
  • Where they dug in. Wikipedia puts the hollow 800 to 900 yards south-east of Snipe; Miskimon, south.
  • The tanks destroyed. Turner's citation counts not less than 90 German tanks attacking, 35 set on fire and at least 20 more immobilised. The committee that went over the ground a month later, as Lucas Phillips gives it, counted at least 32 tanks burnt out (21 German, 11 Italian) and 5 self-propelled guns, with 15 or 20 more knocked out and recovered. Wikipedia gives the committee 22 German and 10 Italian tanks. Pitt allows 34 tanks and self-propelled guns.
  • The losses. Lucas Phillips gives 72 riflemen and gunners killed and wounded, the sappers' loss not known. The New Zealand official history says fewer than 100 of about 300.
  • The withdrawal. The New Zealand history says the guns were wrecked and the men started back at about 21:00. Wikipedia gives 22:30; Miskimon says they waited until 23:00 for leave to go.
  • When the attacks began. Turner's citation has the position attacked from 05:30; Miskimon has the guns open at about 06:00.
  • Turner's rank. The New Zealand history calls him "Major V. B. Turner"; the Gazette names him a lieutenant-colonel, a temporary rank.

A hat trick

At about 13:00 eight Italian tanks and a self-propelled gun came at the south-west side of the hollow. One six-pounder could still fire there: Sergeant Charles Calistan's. Turner went to it with Lieutenant Jack Toms. Toms ran 100 yards to his jeep for more shells; the jeep was hit and caught fire, but he got the boxes to the gun. Turner loaded, and was wounded in the head; he refused to be seen to until the last tank was hit. Calistan's gun set the tanks on fire one after another, and Turner is said to have called out "a hat trick". Calistan received the DCM to go with his MM. He had been put up for the VC.

How the field is drawn

Snipe, 27 October 1942, at 10 m a hex: 200 x 160 hexes, about 2000 m west to east and 1390 m north to south, north at the top: the oval hollow of Snipe in the middle (open ground, ringed by the objective), the low ridges to the west and east, flat desert with camelthorn all round. The hollow is drawn to the accounts' size; its depth, the ridges and the guns' places inside their company sectors are ours. The Axis attacks the accounts number are drawn at those numbers; the rest, and where each came from, are ours, with round numbers. A tank unit is four men to a tank. Panzers play as heavy armour, the Italian M13s, M14s and Semoventi as light. The British artillery is not on call (the observer was lost at 04:00), and the friendly fire is not played. Clock: GMT+3. The camelthorn is not drawn: the rules' scrub would keep tanks out of it, and it stopped none here.

The Rangers at Cisterna, 30 January 1944

  • The armies: Americans and Germans.
  • Fought for: the edge of Cisterna, attacked by the Americans.
  • The field: 150 by 120 hexes of 10 m, about 1,500 by 1,040 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, calm or light air from the north.
  • Wounds: WWII 1941-45 - hospitalized (Owens comparison set).
  • On the travel map: Anzio, 1944 (the beachhead to Cisterna), at Cisterna.

The campaign

By January 1944 the Fifth Army in Italy was held at the Gustav Line, in front of Cassino. To turn the line, the US VI Corps under Major General John P. Lucas landed behind it at Anzio and Nettuno on 22 January 1944. Its task was to take the Alban Hills and cut the roads that fed the German line. The landing was almost unopposed, and Colonel William O. Darby's 6615th Ranger Force, the 1st, 3rd and 4th Ranger Battalions, took the port of Anzio nearly intact.

The Germans moved faster than the Allies. The Fourteenth Army took over the defence on 25 January, and the Hermann Göring Division blocked the roads inland. The 3rd Infantry Division, under Major General Lucian K. Truscott, attacked towards Cisterna from 25 to 27 January and was stopped about three miles short. With some 71,500 Germans reckoned against 61,332 of his own men ashore, Lucas planned a general attack for 30 January, before the odds grew worse.

In the 3rd Division's plan, the 1st and 3rd Rangers were to slip through the German line in the dark, about four miles across the fields, and seize Cisterna and Highway 7 by surprise. The 4th Rangers and the 3rd Battalion, 15th Infantry were to follow up the road, and the 7th and 15th Infantry to attack on the flanks at 02:00. Patrols suggested the German line in front of the town was not yet firm.

The places

  • Anzio and Nettuno: the two small ports where VI Corps came ashore.
  • The Mussolini Canal: the drainage canal across the reclaimed Pontine marshes; its west branch was the start line.
  • The Pantano ditch: the drainage ditch that ran north-west across the fields, east of the Conca road, and gave the Rangers cover.
  • The Conca–Cisterna road: the road north to the town, up which the 4th Rangers attacked.
  • Isola Bella: the hamlet on the road below Cisterna, held by machine guns in farmhouses.
  • Femina Morta: the place on the road where the 4th Rangers were stopped.
  • The Calcaprini house: a farm where German self-propelled guns were in bivouac, which the column had to pass.
  • Cisterna: the town on Highway 7, the old Via Appia, and the railway. It stayed in German hands until May 1944.
  • Rome: where captured Rangers were marched past the Colosseum.

The leaders

  • William O. Darby (American, Ranger Force): raised the 1st Ranger Battalion in 1942. He followed the fight by radio from his command post near the start line.
  • Jack Dobson (American, 1st Ranger Battalion): newly in command; he led the column to the edge of the town and was wounded.
  • Alvah Miller (American, 3rd Ranger Battalion): newly in command; killed by a German tank round near dawn.
  • Roy A. Murray (American, 4th Ranger Battalion): his attack up the road was held all day short of Isola Bella.
  • Robert E. Ehalt (American, 3rd Ranger Battalion): the senior NCO who sent the last message from the perimeter.
  • Lucian K. Truscott (American, 3rd Infantry Division): planned the attack, with the Rangers in the lead.
  • John P. Lucas (American, VI Corps): ordered the general attack of 30 January.
  • Eberhard von Mackensen (German, Fourteenth Army): was preparing his own counter-attack from round Cisterna.
  • Paul Conrath (German, Hermann Göring Division): commanded the division that held the town.

The battle

The 1st Rangers crossed the start line in the dark and the 3rd followed about 15 minutes behind, each man with two bandoliers of ammunition and many grenades. They went in single file along the Pantano ditch, past German posts they could see and hear. Sentries walked the bank above them more than once. The column broke in two on the way, and four of the 3rd Battalion's radio operators lost themselves. Major Miller was killed as dawn came.

At first light the head of the column was within 800 yards of Cisterna. Stewart has the alarm raised at about 06:10, when a German sentry screamed as he was knifed. The Rangers ran on through a German bivouac. Then a force led by three self-propelled guns opened fire; the Rangers knocked the guns out. As the light grew, machine guns, mortars and snipers in houses, haystacks and dugouts pinned them in the open, treeless fields. By about 07:10, Stewart says, the battalions were in a crescent-shaped hasty defence. At 07:30 the 1st Battalion broke radio silence. At about 08:30 a few Rangers reached the buildings by the railway station.

Behind them a platoon of 43 men of the 3rd Reconnaissance Troop, sent up the road, ran into a road block; one man got back. The 4th Rangers were stopped by machine guns in the farmhouses below Isola Bella. Darby sent two tank destroyers and two half-tracks to break through; two ran onto mines.

The Germans had brought fresh troops in the night before. The 2nd Parachute Lehr Battalion came up during the fight, with tanks, flak wagons and guns firing over open sights. The Rangers ran short of ammunition. Their wounded were carried back as the perimeter shrank. About noon German tanks came down from Highway 7 and drove back and forth through the positions, firing along the ditches, and split the Rangers into small groups. They answered with bazookas and sticky grenades, and Dobson counted 15 armoured vehicles burning. Paratroops then marched captured Rangers towards the perimeter; when Rangers shot two guards, the Germans bayoneted two prisoners. The surrender began to spread. Between 12:15 and 12:30 the last message came, and the line was gone.

Of 767 men in the two battalions, six came back. Most of the rest were taken. The Germans carried away the wounded and sent the others by lorry to collecting points. Lawrence Gilbert, of the 1st Battalion, remembered prisoners paraded past the Colosseum in Rome for German cameras. The 3rd Battalion, 15th Infantry, sent after the Rangers, took Isola Bella once they had surrendered.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The clock. None of the accounts says which clock it used. Italy and the German army both kept GMT+1 that winter (tz database). On it the sun rose at Cisterna about 07:23 and civil dawn came about 06:54 (our reckoning), later than the "first light" King gives at about 05:45.
  • The start. Stewart has the 1st Rangers cross the start line at 01:00. The Army's Anzio Beachhead has them cross the west branch of the canal at about 01:30, and Laurie says they moved out at 01:30. King dates the Force command post's move to 23:15 on 30 January, a day late.
  • Who was waiting. Anzio Beachhead says the Germans had brought in fresh troops the night before and had apparently found the column. Laurie says men of the 715th Motorized Infantry Division found it in the night and laid an ambush at first light. Stewart rules out an ambush: the infiltration worked, he says, and the Rangers struck a defence that was already there. King puts the failure down to intelligence; a Polish deserter who warned of the build-up was sent to the rear unheard.
  • The last message. Anzio Beachhead gives 1st Sergeant Ehalt's last message at 12:30. Stewart gives 12:15 and calls him sergeant major, as does King.
  • The losses. King, Laurie and Anzio Beachhead give six of 767 back and no split. Haskew gives 311 killed and 450 captured. World War II Day by Day gives 12 killed, 36 wounded and 743 captured. Stewart says more than 740 were killed or captured.
  • The date. Wikipedia's article on the battle has the Rangers set out on 31 January; the Army histories say the night of 29/30 January.

We are awfully sorry

Darby followed the fight from his command post by radio. The last voice from the perimeter was Robert Ehalt's, of the 3rd Battalion. He reported the 1st Battalion's commander wounded, the 3rd Battalion's executive officer killed, and German tanks closing in. He had about ten men with him and had lost touch with the companies. Darby told him he would stay with them to the end. Stewart gives Ehalt's last words as "Some of the fellows are giving up. Colonel, we are awfully sorry." Ehalt smashed his radio as the tanks came up and fought on until he surrendered.

How the field is drawn

The Rangers short of Cisterna at first light, 30 January 1944, at 10 m a hex: 150 x 120 hexes, about 1500 m east to west and 1040 m north to south, north at the top: the southern edge of Cisterna along the top, the railroad station top left, the Conca road coming up from the bottom left, the Pantano ditch from the bottom right, and open, treeless fields with farmhouses and haystacks. The fields, the ditch, the road, the farmhouses and the town's edge are drawn by hand to the shape the account gives, not traced from any map; the deployment is first light, in our own words, with round numbers for play. A cold, still January dawn; the reclaimed ground soft. There are no vehicle rules: the self-propelled guns and tanks are on call as direct fire (Fire support), and the Rangers' bazookas and sticky grenades are left to the GM. The Germans in houses, haystacks and dugouts start gone to ground; houses are buildings (cover).

The phases

From exchange Phase What happens
1 Caught at first light About 06:10, short of the town, a German sentry cries out as he is knifed and the column is discovered; at dawn three self-propelled guns open on it.

Where the sources disagree on something the battle turns on, the field map asks which account to fight (or rolls it, each as likely). The first is the game's own, and the enemy commander's benchmark is run on it; a battle on another is scored against history only.
