Snakeshead Ridge and the abbey, 17-18 February 1944

  • The armies: Allies and Germans.
  • Fought for: Point 593, attacked by the Allies.
  • The field: 200 by 150 hexes of 10 m, about 2,000 by 1,300 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, breeze from the north, night.
  • Wounds: WWII 1941-45 - hospitalized (Owens comparison set).
  • On the travel map: Cassino, 1944 (Monte Cairo to the Liri valley), at Point 593 (Monte Calvario).
  • The record: the fight lasted about 418 exchanges (a minute each).

The campaign

By January 1944 the Fifth Army under General Mark Clark faced the Gustav Line, the German line across Italy along the Garigliano and Rapido rivers. At Cassino it barred the Liri valley, the way to Rome, which was just over 10 kilometres wide and overlooked by Monte Cassino, about 500 metres high, with the Benedictine abbey on top (NZHistory). The Fifth Army reached the line on 15 January after six weeks of fighting that had cost it about 16,000 men (Majdalany).

The first battle was meant to draw German reserves away from the landing at Anzio on 22 January. The British 10 Corps crossed the Garigliano from 17 January. On the night of 20 January the US 36th Division tried to cross the Rapido near Sant'Angelo and was thrown back; the 141st Infantry withdrew at daybreak on the 21st, and a second try on the 21st also failed (Blumenson). From 24 January the 34th Division crossed north of the town, took the Italian barracks and Monte Castellone, and fought along the ridges towards the abbey. One battalion reached Monte Albaneta, a little more than a mile north-west of the abbey, and another came within several hundred yards of it before it was driven back. By 10 February the 168th Infantry's three battalions had 154, 393 and 246 effective men (Blumenson).

Alexander and Clark had agreed that if the Americans had not broken the line by 12 February, a New Zealand Corps under Lieutenant General Bernard Freyberg would take over. It had been formed on 3 February from the 2nd New Zealand Division and the 4th Indian Division (Blumenson). Major General Francis Tuker of the 4th Indian Division judged that the abbey must be destroyed before his men attacked, and Freyberg asked for bombers on 12 February. Clark did not think it a military necessity, but Alexander left the decision to Freyberg, and General Wilson approved it after Generals Eaker and Devers reported seeing soldiers and a radio aerial (Blumenson).

On the morning of 15 February the bombers came. Blumenson has the first of about 250 attack at 09:45 and almost 600 tons dropped, and the whole top of the mountain turned to rubble. Hapgood and Richardson find that the only people killed in the abbey were about 230 Italian civilians sheltering there. The abbot and most of the monks survived in the crypt (Rickard). The bombing came a day and a half before the Indians were ready to attack (NZHistory).

The places

  • Monte Cassino: the mountain above the town, with the abbey founded by St Benedict on its top.
  • Snakeshead Ridge: the narrow crest, about 1,200 yards long with deep ravines on either side, along which the Indians attacked (The Tiger Triumphs).
  • Point 593: the height at the western tip of the ridge, with the ruins of an old fort; the Poles later called it Monte Calvario.
  • Point 444 or 445: the knoll below the abbey that the Gurkhas made for; The Tiger Triumphs calls it Point 445.
  • The copse: the thorn scrub on the slope below the ridge, mined and wired, where the 1/2nd Gurkhas were caught.
  • Monte Castellone and Albaneta: the heights to the north and north-west taken or reached by the Americans in early February.
  • Cassino railway station: south of the town, taken by the 28th (Maori) Battalion on the night of 17 February and lost the next day.
  • The Rapido: the river in front of the town, flooded by the Germans.

The leaders

  • Bernard Freyberg (Allies, New Zealand Corps): asked for the bombing and called it, in Blumenson's report, "his considered opinion that it is a military necessity".
  • Francis Tuker (Allies, 4th Indian Division): had decided that the abbey must be destroyed before his men attacked; he gave up command through illness on 4 February.
  • Harry Dimoline (Allies, 4th Indian Division): commanded the division in Tuker's place.
  • O. de T. Lovett (Allies, 7th Indian Brigade): his brigade, the Royal Sussex, Punjabis and 1/2nd Gurkhas, held the ridge.
  • Lieutenant Colonel Showers (Allies, 1/2nd Gurkha Rifles): badly wounded in the copse.
  • Mark Clark (Allies, Fifth Army): opposed the bombing but deferred to Alexander.
  • Fridolin von Senger und Etterlin (German, XIV Panzer Corps): said after the war that no German troops had been inside the abbey before the bombing.
  • Ernst-Günther Baade (German, 90th Panzer Grenadier Division): in charge of all troops in the Cassino position from 1 February.

The battle

The bombing did not take the hill. Bombs fell short on the Indian posts on Snakeshead Ridge, and the forward posts had been drawn back. The two lines were so close that the guns could not fire a barrage for the infantry (The Tiger Triumphs). Point 593 was made the first objective. On the night of 15 February one company of the 1st Royal Sussex went for it and was stopped by a palisade of boulders about 70 yards on; it came back with 20 casualties. On the 16th the whole battalion attacked. By 22:00 it was on the approaches, and Lieutenant Dennis Cox led a charge into the ruined fort. Then a German flare was read as an order to withdraw, and before dawn the Sussex gave the place up. Holmes counts the battalion's loss over the two nights at 12 of 15 officers and 162 of 313 men.

The next attack was a divisional one. At midnight on 17 February the 4/6th Rajputana Rifles, with three Sussex companies, went for Point 593. Major Markham Lee reached the crest with a handful of men and died there. By 03:30 the attack had stopped. About 02:00 the 1/2nd and 1/9th Gurkhas went down the slopes for the abbey. The leading companies of the 1/2nd ran into the copse, which no one had scouted. It was sown with mines and trip-wires and covered by machine guns, and two-thirds of the leading companies were hit within five minutes. Men lay dead with four or more trip-wires round their legs. The other companies, with men of the 1/9th, went round the left of the copse, and shortly before dawn a company got a lodgement on Point 445 (The Tiger Triumphs).

At 04:30 a fourth Rajputana company was thrown in and failed to take the summit, and the Germans won back part of the crest. To move by day would have been suicide, and the Gurkhas came back from Point 445 after dark. Wikipedia gives the Rajputanas' loss as 196, the 1/9th's as 149 and the 1/2nd's as 96. In the valley the Maori had taken the station, but no bridge could be built behind them, and German tanks drove them out on the afternoon of the 18th. Dimoline and Freyberg called the attack off that day.

In the copse Naik Bir Bahadur Thapa, hit in about a dozen places, got through to the far side with a few survivors and held on there. Only a handful came back at dawn. The Tiger Triumphs says nothing of the aid posts; it names the stretcher-bearers who went back into the scrub for the wounded.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The clock. None of the accounts says which clock it used. Italy and the German army both kept GMT+1 that winter (tz database).
  • The bombing. Blumenson has about 250 bombers from 09:45 and almost 600 tons. The Tiger Triumphs has 15 waves from 08:00 and 35 tons in the morning and afternoon. Laurie, cited by Wikipedia, gives 142 B-17s, 47 B-25s and 40 B-26s; Wikipedia gives 1,150 tonnes in its text and 1,400 in its introduction.
  • The dead in the abbey. Hapgood and Richardson give about 230 civilians. Rickard gives 280 to 300 refugees. A civilian witness quoted by Blumenson said some 2,500 people had been inside; the abbot spoke of hundreds of innocent people killed.
  • Were the Germans inside? Senger said not, and the Fifth Army's Counter Intelligence Corps found it unoccupied on 26 February (Blumenson). Eaker and Devers reported soldiers and an aerial. Paratroops moved into the ruins after the abbot left on 17 February (Rickard).
  • Short bombs. The Tiger Triumphs and Blumenson give 24 Indian casualties; General Walker heard of about 40.
  • The second Sussex night. The Tiger Triumphs has the fort taken and given up over a misread flare. Blumenson has five battalions regain the lost ground and be driven back by counter-attacks at daybreak.
  • The Gurkhas' hill. The Tiger Triumphs names Point 445; other accounts give Point 444.
  • The Rajputana and Gurkha losses. The figures in Wikipedia have no source given.

Sixteen times

Sher Bahadur Thapa was a stretcher-bearer of the 1/2nd Gurkha Rifles. On the night of 17-18 February his battalion's leading companies were caught in a mined copse below Point 593, under machine-gun fire, with men falling over trip-wires in the dark. Two-thirds of them were hit within five minutes. Sher Bahadur went into the scrub after the wounded and brought them out, and went back again. The Tiger Triumphs says that he crossed the copse no fewer than sixteen times. He was killed soon afterwards.

Hill 700, Bougainville, 8-12 March 1944

  • The armies: Americans and Japanese.
  • Fought for: the saddle in the line, attacked by the Japanese.
  • The field: 120 by 100 hexes of 10 m, about 1,200 by 870 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Rain, calm or light air from the south-east.
  • Wounds: Bougainville 1944 - all hits.
  • On the travel map: Bougainville, 1944 (the Torokina perimeter), at Hill 700.
  • The record: the fight lasted about 4171 exchanges (a minute each).

The campaign

In early November 1943 the 3rd Marine Division and the 37th Infantry Division landed at Empress Augusta Bay, on the west coast of Bougainville. They held a perimeter round Cape Torokina and built airfields there, within reach of Rabaul. By March 1944 the XIV Corps under Major General Oscar Griswold held it with the 37th and Americal Divisions: about 27,000 combat troops, and about 62,000 men in all (Miller).

General Hitoshi Imamura at Rabaul and Lieutenant General Harukichi Hyakutake of the 17th Army planned one blow against it. Hyakutake thought he faced about 30,000 men, a third of them airfield ground crew. His main force was Lieutenant General Masatane Kanda's 6th Division, with battalions of the 17th Division. Guns came along the coast by barge at night; the infantry marched inland with about two weeks' rations. Patrols, prisoners, radio intercepts and captured papers warned the Americans.

The plan had three groups. The Iwasa Unit, the 23rd Infantry and the 2nd Battalion, 13th Infantry, under Major General Shun Iwasa, was to take Hill 700 on 8 March. The Muda and Magata Units were to strike further east and west, and all were to reach the Torokina airstrip by 17 March.

The places

  • Hill 700: the highest ground the Americans held, on the north side of the perimeter. Its slopes ran at 65 to 75 per cent (Miller).
  • The saddle: the low ground between the two knobs of Hill 700, where the 23rd Infantry broke in.
  • Cannon Hill: the next height, held by the 3rd Battalion, 145th Infantry.
  • McClelland Road: the supply road behind the hill, under Japanese fire from 9 March.
  • The Piva airfields: the bomber and fighter strips inside the perimeter.
  • Hill 260: the Americal Division's outpost to the east, attacked from 10 March.
  • Blue Ridge and Hills 250, 600 and 1111: Japanese-held heights to the north, with their guns.
  • The 21st Evacuation Hospital: about 4,000 yards behind the front at its nearest point.

The leaders

  • Harukichi Hyakutake (Japanese, 17th Army): planned the attack and underestimated the Americans by about half.
  • Masatane Kanda (Japanese, 6th Division): his division made up most of the attacking force. His answers after the war are one of Miller's sources.
  • Shun Iwasa (Japanese, Iwasa Unit): a major general, commander of the force sent against Hill 700.
  • Oscar Griswold (American, XIV Corps): judged the perimeter as well organised as the men and ground allowed, and sent reserves to the 145th from 10 March.
  • Robert S. Beightler (American, 37th Division): released the 1st Battalion, 145th, on 9 March and brought in the 2nd Battalion, 148th.
  • Cecil B. Whitcomb (American, 145th Infantry): relieved on 11 March after the assistant division commander, Brigadier General Charles F. Craig, reported him suffering from "extreme battle fatigue" (Miller).
  • Herb Radcliffe (American, 2nd Battalion, 148th Infantry): a lieutenant colonel; his battalion retook the saddle.
  • Clinton S. McLaughlin (American, G Company, 145th): wounded twice, he held his position on 11 March and won the Distinguished Service Cross.

The battle

Japanese guns opened on 8 March. Miller has the first rounds at 05:45; Frankel, about 06:00. They fell mostly on the Piva airfields. The 23rd Infantry spent the day moving up, and did not attack. American guns fired on its assembly areas for two hours from about noon, and Frankel says the 3rd Battalion, 23rd Infantry, was nearly wiped out.

The 2nd Battalion, 145th, held the hill with E and G Companies in line and F Company in reserve. Shortly after midnight, in rain, about two companies came up the north slope against G Company's 1st Platoon and E Company on the summit. They were driven off. At about 02:30 on 9 March the 23rd came again in column of battalions, the 2nd Battalion leading. It blew the wire with bangalore torpedoes, knocked out a pillbox and reached the saddle. It took seven pillboxes, and by noon held a salient about 100 yards wide and 50 deep.

At about noon C Company, 145th, attacked up the south slope, with two platoons of F Company from the flanks. Two M3 light tanks of the 754th Tank Battalion tried to help that afternoon but could not climb the hill. By 17:35 F Company had retaken five pillboxes. Japanese fire closed McClelland Road, and carrying parties took ammunition up and the wounded down by hand.

The Japanese attacked again at 06:45 on 10 March. One engineer bangalore went off among its own men and killed four. At 17:00 men of the 1st and 2nd Battalions attacked with bangalores, rocket launchers and pole charges. They took several pillboxes and lost them again. That night the Japanese came on in close-packed waves and took one more pillbox at the saddle.

On 11 March Whitcomb was relieved and his executive officer, Colonel Freer, took over. At 13:20 the 2nd Battalion, 148th, attacked the saddle after a short bombardment; one platoon reached the crest but lost eight dead. On 12 March E and F Companies, 148th, went in with grenades, rifles, flamethrowers and rocket launchers. The last pillbox fell at 13:17, and by 15:30 the line was whole. The Americans counted 309 Japanese bodies there, and the Iwasa Unit withdrew on 13 March.

The wounded went down by litter, a carry of 1,200 yards, then by half-track and jeep ambulance to the 21st Evacuation Hospital. A Surgeon General's team under Colonel Ashley W. Oughterson studied the Allied casualties on the island from 15 February to 21 April 1944. It arrived on 22 March, after Hill 700, and worked from graves registration files, hospital records and talks with aidmen; from 23 March it autopsied the dead. Of 1,788 casualties, mortars caused 38.8 per cent and rifles 24.9 per cent, but machine guns killed 57.6 per cent of the men they hit. Head wounds were 21.5 per cent, more than in past wars. The study was printed as chapter V of Wound Ballistics (1962). The game's Bougainville tables come from its counts.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The clock and the first shells. The times are from American records; no source says which clock was kept, and no Japanese times were found in English. Miller has the Japanese guns open at 05:45 on 8 March; Frankel, 06:00; the Ohio National Guard historian, 06:27.
  • Who held the hill. Miller has the 2nd Battalion, 145th. The Wikipedia article says the 2nd and 3rd Battalions; Frankel puts the 3rd on Cannon Hill.
  • The salient. Miller gives about 100 yards wide and 50 deep; Frankel, 70 yards wide and 50 deep; the wound study, 75 yards deep on a 100-yard front.
  • The last attack. Miller has the last pillbox fall at 13:17 on 12 March and the line restored by 15:30. Frankel has E and F Companies, 148th, start at 08:00 and the hill regained by 16:00. The Ohio National Guard has them go over the top at 12:30.
  • Japanese strength. Miller gives 15,000 to 19,000 for the whole offensive; Kanda later said 19,000 and about 2,000 sailors. Shindo says only 9,548 were committed. No source read gives the Iwasa Unit's strength.
  • Japanese dead at Hill 700. Miller gives 309 counted at the saddle. Frankel says about 1,500 were buried on the reverse slope. The wound study gives 2,219: 719 counted and 1,500 estimated.
  • American losses. Miller gives the 37th Division 5 officers and 73 men killed from 8 to 13 March; the Ohio National Guard adds about 400 wounded. The wound study counts 2,600 men engaged on Hill 700 and 519 casualties, 61 of them dead.
  • The whole offensive. Miller gives over 5,000 Japanese killed, more than 3,000 wounded and 263 American dead. James estimates 3,500 Japanese killed; Shindo, 2,700.

They would not be ordered

On 9 March Japanese fire covered the road behind Hill 700. Ambulances of A and B Collecting Companies, 112th Medical Battalion, waited at G Company's motor pool with the wounded. Colonel Whitcomb told the drivers he would not order them to run the road. Eight went anyway, and brought their casualties back. Two drivers, Bob Pittman and "Doc" Davis, were lightly hit by mortar fragments. Private Joe Bernard of A Company was hit by two snipers, and his orderly was wounded. After that, Frankel says, 17 half-tracks shuttled between the line and the aid stations.

How the field is drawn

Hill 700 on the Torokina perimeter, Bougainville, March 1944, at 10 m a hex: 120 x 100 hexes, about 1200 m east to west and 870 m north to south, north at the top: the ridge across the middle with a saddle between two knobs, the American pillbox line on its forward crest, wire and a cleared belt below it, and jungle beyond. The ridge, the saddle, the clearing and the line are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is the start of the attack, in our own words, with round numbers for play. Pillboxes are bunkers (cover 50%); the wire is slow to cross.

Cassino town and Castle Hill, 15 March 1944

  • The armies: Allies and Germans.
  • Fought for: Castle Hill, attacked by the Allies.
  • The field: 140 by 120 hexes of 10 m, about 1,400 by 1,040 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Overcast, breeze from the south.
  • Wounds: WWII 1941-45 - hospitalized (Owens comparison set).
  • On the travel map: Cassino, 1944 (Monte Cairo to the Liri valley), at Cassino.
  • The record: the fight lasted about 10801 exchanges (a minute each).

The campaign

The New Zealand Corps' first attack failed on 18 February 1944. Freyberg planned the next one from the north, through the town of Cassino itself, after a bombing of the town as heavy as the one that had fallen on the abbey. Rain put it off for more than three weeks; the 6th New Zealand Brigade's attack, first set for 24 February, waited for weather fit for the bombers (Wikipedia, citing Puttick). On 2 March Major General Howard Kippenberger, commanding the New Zealand Division, lost both feet to a mine, and Brigadier G. B. Parkinson took over (NZHistory).

The Germans used the wait. The 1st Parachute Division under General Richard Heidrich took over from the 15th Panzer Grenadier Division. The Tiger Triumphs counts seven paratroop battalions on Monastery Hill and in the town, three more in reserve, and about 180 guns behind them. In the town the paratroops had cellars and steel shelters that the bombs did not break.

The plan was for the 6th New Zealand Brigade to take Castle Hill and clear the town, with tanks of the 19th Armoured Regiment, while the 5th Indian Brigade climbed from Castle Hill by the hairpin bends of the road to Hangman's Hill, below the abbey. On the night of 14 March the New Zealanders drew back from the edge of the town to clear it for the bombers. The Tiger Triumphs says that the signal "Bradman will be batting to-morrow" may have puzzled the German listeners.

The places

  • Cassino: the town at the foot of Monte Cassino, on Route 6 (Highway 6), the road to Rome.
  • Castle Hill (Point 193): the rock above the north-west of the town, with the ruined castle of Rocca Janula.
  • Points 165 and 236: the lower and upper hairpin bends of the road from Castle Hill towards the abbey.
  • Point 202: a knoll on the slope, held by a New Zealand company until 24 March.
  • Hangman's Hill (Point 435): a rocky platform below the abbey with the concrete pylon of an aerial ropeway on it, about 250 yards from the ruins.
  • The Continental Hotel: on Route 6 at the foot of the hill; the paratroops held it to the end.
  • The railway station: south of the town, lost by the Maori in February and taken by the New Zealanders on 17 March.
  • Venafro: a town about 10 air miles away, bombed in error on 15 March.

The leaders

  • Bernard Freyberg (Allies, New Zealand Corps): planned the attack and recommended stopping it on 23 March.
  • G. B. Parkinson (Allies, New Zealand Division): commanded the division after Kippenberger was wounded.
  • John McDuff (Allies, 25th Battalion): his battalion led the attack into the town.
  • Major Beckett (Allies, 1/4th Essex): twice wounded, held the castle walls against the paratroops' charge.
  • Colonel Nangle (Allies, 1/9th Gurkha Rifles): sent his companies up to Hangman's Hill.
  • Captain Drinkall (Allies, C Company, 1/9th Gurkhas): led his company through the dark to Hangman's Hill.
  • Colonel Noble (Allies, 1/4th Essex): killed by a sniper on Castle Hill after the charge.
  • Richard Heidrich (German, 1st Parachute Division): held the town and the abbey.
  • Heinrich von Vietinghoff (German, Tenth Army): ordered the massif held "at all costs" at 10:40 on 15 March (Blumenson).

The battle

Blumenson has the medium bombers over the town at 08:30 and the heavy bombers from 08:45, in waves about every 15 minutes until noon: 435 aircraft and nearly 1,000 tons of bombs, of which only about 300 tons fell in the town. At noon the guns took over. Blumenson counts 746 guns and howitzers, firing almost 200,000 rounds between 12:20 and 20:00. Short bombs killed 28 Allied soldiers and wounded more; at Venafro bombs killed 17 soldiers and 40 civilians.

The 25th Battalion went into the rubble from the north with the 19th Armoured Regiment's tanks. Craters 40 to 50 feet across and heaps of masonry stopped the tanks, and paratroops came up from the cellars and fired from the ruins. About four hours after the infantry moved, Castle Hill was taken (The Tiger Triumphs). The 25th Battalion was to clear the west of the town as far as the Continental Hotel, and did not reach it (Wikipedia). That evening the rain came, and the craters filled. Blumenson says no tank could pass for about 36 hours.

At dusk the 1/4th Essex took over Castle Hill, and a company reached Point 165. The 1/6th Rajputana Rifles came up under fire; their headquarters was hit and their colonel wounded. At 01:30 Colonel Nangle sent two Gurkha companies forward; one lost 15 men in a minute, and Drinkall's C Company passed the castle and disappeared into the night. At midday on the 16th a faint wireless message showed that it held Hangman's Hill (The Tiger Triumphs). On the night of 16-17 March the rest of the 1/9th Gurkhas joined it, passing the Continental Hotel in the dark.

The fighting in the town went on from house to house. On 17 March the New Zealanders took the station. Each rifle company of the 25th Battalion was down to about 50 men. One morning, as the night thinned, a battalion of the 1st Parachute Regiment came down the spur from the abbey, overran the posts at the hairpin bend and reached the castle walls. The Essex and the gunners of 1st Field Regiment held them there with grenades and tommy-guns at point-blank range (The Tiger Triumphs gives no date). On 19 March a tank thrust behind the massif lost about a dozen tanks. On the 21st the 21st Battalion's attack down Route 6 was caught in crossfire near the Continental Hotel (Phillips). The attack was given up on 23 March. On the night of 24 March the men on Hangman's Hill came down: 10 officers and 247 other ranks (The Tiger Triumphs).

The wounded from Castle Hill were carried along a track under fire and over the escarpment to ambulances on the Rapido, many of them driven by American Field Service volunteers over a route of about five miles (The Tiger Triumphs).

Where the accounts disagree

  • The clock. None of the accounts says which clock it used. Italy and the German army both kept GMT+1 that winter (tz database).
  • The bombers and guns. Blumenson gives 435 aircraft, nearly 1,000 tons and 746 guns. Rickard gives 435 aircraft, 1,000 tons and about 750 guns. The Tiger Triumphs gives 610 guns and about 1,200 tons of shell. Wikipedia says nearly 500 aircraft were planned and gives 750 tonnes of bombs (Laurie).
  • Castle Hill. The Tiger Triumphs, NZHistory and the 25th Battalion's history have it taken on 15 March; Rickard puts it on the 17th.
  • The 26th Battalion. Blumenson says the New Zealanders could not reach Highway 6; Rickard has the 26th held up north of it.
  • The end. Blumenson, The Tiger Triumphs and NZHistory give 23 March; Rickard has Alexander cancel it on the 22nd.
  • The losses. Blumenson gives about 2,000 New Zealand and Indian losses in nine days: almost 300 killed, nearly 250 missing and more than 1,500 wounded. Wikipedia gives about 3,000 for the 4th Indian Division and 1,600 for the New Zealanders. The Tiger Triumphs says the 4th Indian Division lost 4,000 men at Cassino; NZHistory gives 343 New Zealand dead by early April. The paratroops' 2nd Battalion, 3rd Parachute Regiment lost half its men and still held (Rickard); Blumenson says about 300 men in a tunnel came through the bombing.

Scissors and a pocket-knife

Edmond Hazle and Leonard Piper were lance-corporals of the 1/4th Essex. They went up to Hangman's Hill with the men who joined the Gurkhas there, below the abbey and cut off from the rest of the division. For eight days, supplied only by air drops and porters at night, the garrison held on. Hazle and Piper stayed with the wounded the whole time. The Tiger Triumphs says that Hazle cut off shattered limbs with scissors and a pocket-knife. He already held the Distinguished Conduct Medal and was given a bar to it.

How the field is drawn

The town of Cassino and Castle Hill on 15 March 1944, at 10 m a hex: 140 x 120 hexes, about 1400 m east to west and 1040 m north to south, north at the top: the bombed town in the middle, Castle Hill and its ruined castle at the upper left, the massif's foot rising to the abbey along the left edge, the road from Caira coming in from the north, Route 6 and the station to the south, the Rapido along the right. The ruins, craters, castle and roads are drawn by hand, not traced from any map or photograph; the deployment is the attack going in, in our own words, with round numbers for play. The town is rubble (rubble) with flooded craters (marsh): tanks can keep only to the open road and the fields, and the paratroops' cellars are bunkers. Overcast, the ground already wet; that evening the rain came down.

The Poles at Point 593 and Phantom Ridge, 12 May 1944

  • The armies: Allies and Germans.
  • Fought for: Point 593, attacked by the Allies.
  • The field: 200 by 150 hexes of 10 m, about 2,000 by 1,300 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, calm or light air, night.
  • Wounds: WWII 1941-45 - hospitalized (Owens comparison set).
  • On the travel map: Cassino, 1944 (Monte Cairo to the Liri valley), at Phantom Ridge.

The campaign

After the March battle failed, General Sir Harold Alexander gathered his armies for one offensive along the whole front, Operation Diadem. It was timed to fall close to the landing in Normandy, so that the German divisions in Italy would be held there. Four corps were to attack: from right to left, the II Polish Corps and the British 13 Corps of the Eighth Army, then the French Expeditionary Corps and the US II Corps of the Fifth Army (Wikipedia). 13 Corps was to cross the Rapido in the valley below Monte Cassino; the Poles were to take the massif from the north, the task in which the Americans, the Indians and the New Zealanders had failed.

Lieutenant General Władysław Anders's corps was about 50,000 strong (Wikipedia). It held the right of 13 Corps with two infantry divisions, the 3rd Carpathian and the 5th Kresowa, of two brigades each, and an armoured brigade (Fisher). Opposite stood the 1st Parachute Division, which still held the abbey and the town. The US Army staff study of 1984 places the 3rd Parachute Regiment on Monte Cassino and the heights beside it, and the 100th Mountain Regiment round Monte Castellone and Colle Sant'Angelo.

At 23:00 on 11 May some 1,660 guns opened fire along the front, 1,060 of them on the Eighth Army's (Fisher). At 01:00 on 12 May the Poles went in.

The places

  • Point 593: the height at the north-west end of Snakeshead Ridge, about 1,000 yards north-west of the abbey; the Poles call it Monte Calvario.
  • Point 569: the height beyond 593, taken and lost by the Carpathians on 12 May.
  • Phantom Ridge (Widmo): about 1,800 yards north-west of the abbey (Fisher), the Kresowa Division's objective.
  • Colle Sant'Angelo and Point 575: the heights beyond Phantom Ridge, from which German fire swept the Polish attack.
  • Albaneta: the farm below 593, and the ravine in front of it (the Gardziel, "the gullet") where the 1st Battalion was caught.
  • The Doctor's House: a former hermitage about 250 metres behind the front, the forward dressing station (Polska Zbrojna).
  • Caira: the village at the foot of the hills, with the forward surgical station.
  • The abbey: in ruins since 15 February, still held by the paratroops.

The leaders

  • Władysław Anders (Allies, II Polish Corps): took the task, and at 14:00 on 12 May ordered his divisions back to their start line (Fisher).
  • Bronisław Duch (Allies, 3rd Carpathian Division): his 1st Carpathian Rifle Brigade made the attack on 593 and Albaneta.
  • Nikodem Sulik (Allies, 5th Kresowa Division): afterwards wrote of the shock to his men of losing close comrades and junior officers on Phantom Ridge (montecassino.info.pl).
  • Lieutenant Colonel Domoń (Allies, Kresowa Division): wounded on Phantom Ridge about midday (Dookoła Rzeszy).
  • Sidney Kirkman (Allies, 13 Corps): his divisions fought across the Rapido below the Poles.
  • Richard Heidrich (German, 1st Parachute Division): held the massif and the town.
  • Ludwig Heilmann (German, 3rd Parachute Regiment): commanded the regiment from 15 November 1943 (Traces of War); its 1st Battalion made the counter-attacks on 593.
  • Valentin Feurstein (German, LI Mountain Corps): his corps held a line of about 80 kilometres on 10 May (Dookoła Rzeszy).

The battle

The bombardment stunned the Germans only for a time. On the right the 2nd Battalion of the 1st Carpathian Rifle Brigade went up for Point 593 and took it, about 02:00 according to the Dookoła Rzeszy account and about 02:30 according to warhist.pl. Dookoła Rzeszy has Point 569 taken at 02:50, and reserves of I./Fallschirmjäger-Regiment 3 pushing back at the Poles from 03:15. At 04:28 the brigade's 1st Battalion was ordered into the ravine in front of Albaneta. Two companies got in and were stopped there by crossfire.

On the left the Kresowa Division moved off about 01:30 up the gully towards Phantom Ridge. Its sappers clearing the mines lost about 90% of their men (warhist.pl). The 15th Battalion reached Phantom Ridge about 02:30, having lost about a fifth of its strength, and the 18th Battalion came up by 06:00 into fire from bunkers. A German counter-attack from Albaneta at 11:30 failed; another at 13:00 drove the Poles back (Dookoła Rzeszy).

At daybreak the Poles were in full view of the German guns, mortars and Nebelwerfers on the heights round them and in the abbey. Fisher says their losses became so heavy that they could not stand against the counter-attacks, and that almost half the attackers were killed or wounded. On Point 593 the 2nd Battalion beat off attack after attack; Tadeusz Czerkawski, an ensign there, counted six (Radio Kraków). Point 569 was lost about 11:30. At 14:00 Anders ordered the corps back to its start line after dark. The last men left 593 at 19:30 (warhist.pl).

The wounded were passed back down the hill by hand. Stretcher-bearers stood about every 100 metres along the 2 kilometres from the Doctor's House to the surgical station at Caira, and the journey could take four hours. Dr Alfons Wawrzyniak's team at the Doctor's House treated more than 500 men in the first 24 hours of the attack on 593 (Polska Zbrojna). The corps attacked again on 17 May. That night Kesselring ordered the paratroops off the massif, and on the morning of 18 May a patrol of the 12th Podolian Lancers under 2nd Lieutenant Kazimierz Gurbiel raised the regiment's pennant on the ruins of the abbey (Radio Kraków).

Where the accounts disagree

  • The clock. None of the accounts says which clock it used. Italy and the German army had gone over to summer time, GMT+2, in April 1944 (tz database).
  • When 593 was lost. warhist.pl has the Poles forced off 593 by the fifth counter-attack at about 08:40, and the last defender leave at 19:30. Dookoła Rzeszy has the Germans retake it at 19:00 with the assault guns of Sturmgeschütz-Kompanie 14. Fisher speaks only of a series of counter-attacks. Dookoła Rzeszy also dates the opening a day early, to the night of 10-11 May.
  • The last officer on 593. warhist.pl names 2nd Lieutenant Romański. Other Polish accounts give the name as Radwański or Rynkiewicz.
  • The counter-attacks. Polish reports spoke of a German battalion; Dookoła Rzeszy says it was a platoon.
  • The German regiments. The 1984 staff study puts the 3rd Parachute Regiment on Monte Cassino and the 4th in the town. Wikipedia, citing Whiting, has the Poles attack "Heilmann's 4th Parachute Regiment"; Heilmann commanded the 3rd. Radio Kraków names the 1st Parachute Division and the 5th Mountain Division; Rickard names Kampfgruppe Ruffin in the mountains north-west of the abbey.
  • Who attacked where. Fisher has the Carpathians on 593 and the Kresowa on Phantom Ridge. Radzilowski in The Polish Weekly (2024) gives it the other way round.
  • The losses. Fisher says almost half the attackers were killed or wounded. dzieje.pl gives about 1,800 killed and wounded in the first attack; Monte Cassino Battlefield Tours says some companies lost 40% to 70%. For the whole battle Radio Kraków gives 923 killed, 2,931 wounded and 345 missing; warhist.pl, 924, 2,930 and 345; Wikipedia, citing Whiting, 281 officers and 3,503 other ranks.
  • The flag. dzieje.pl and Lipinski's memoir put the pennant on the ruins at 09:50 on 18 May; Radio Kraków and Wikipedia say 10:20.

Torn shirts

The company medics went up with the infantry, four to a company. Józef Brzeziński was one of them. On Point 593, Polska Zbrojna says, he was wounded three times and kept on, and saved almost 40 men. On Phantom Ridge Ludwik Radziszewski was hit too, and he also carried on dressing the wounded; when his bandages ran out he tore up his shirt to make more. Both men were given the Virtuti Militari, Poland's highest military decoration. Behind them the Doctor's House, 250 metres from the front, treated more than 500 men in the first day.

The phases

From exchange Phase What happens
1 The advance 01:00 on 12 May, after the bombardment: the 1st Battalion goes for Albaneta and the Kresowa for Phantom Ridge.
31 For Point 593 01:30: the 2nd Battalion sets off for Point 593.
61 Point 593 taken About 02:00 to 02:30: Point 593 is taken, then held against counter-attack after counter-attack.
461 Forced off 593 About 08:40 the Poles are forced off 593 by the fifth German attack (one source).
721 Abandon 593 After 13:00 the decision is taken to abandon 593; at 15:00 the 1st Battalion is ordered back.
1111 The last men leave 19:30: the last men of 4th Company leave 593.

A worked example: the section

The Rules follow one medieval retinue. This chapter follows a section of the 1st Newfoundland Regiment at Beaumont-Hamel on 1 July 1916, from St John's Road to the Danger Tree. It uses the same rules and the Modern fire module, and, where dice are rolled, the dice given. The team builder made the section.

The section

The team builder rolls an infantry section of the Newfoundland Regiment. Wilfrid Squires leads it: 3 terms, each a year of the war, so he is 22, with Command 58. Its best shot is Francis White, who fires his rifle at 72%. Its bomber is Edward Snow, and its stretcher-bearer is Joseph Noseworthy, Leechcraft 45. 6 riflemen follow them. Their kit: a steel helmet only, and no body armour.

On the field map

The section: St John's Road

At 09:15 the section leaves St John's Road with the rest of A Company, in extended order: 3 men to a hex, 8 hexes a move, and shots at them count half, as in Modern infantry. The day is fair, and the machine guns of RIR 119 can see them from the moment they cross the crest. Each gun fires 300 rounds a minute, one in 10 rolled as an aimed shot, and its cone falls on the next unit behind. Every serious or critical wound puts a man down, as in Modern fire puts men down, and a light one calls for the stop check.

The gaps in the British wire bunch the men together. Under the guns the section checks at the end of each exchange to see whether it is pinned, with +10 if it has gone to ground. Pinned, it cannot move. Shells burst among them too: a man struck rolls a wound as one hit by shell fragments at 70%, as in Fire support.

In the roller

The heroes' wounds are rolled in full, as in the fight.

The section: the machine gun

A German machine-gunner, a veteran, fires at Francis at 60% and rolls 9: a margin of 51. Against a bullet, a leg takes a margin of 30 or more to be serious, so this one is serious. Francis dodges at 36% and rolls 66: no.

The round strikes his right thigh. It breaks the bone. It bleeds 3, pain 2, and the leg is hurt. The wound carries shock, so he makes a stop check: Nerve 55, less 2 steps of pain, gives 35. He rolls 45 and fails by 10: he can only defend for 2 rounds. At 3 Blood a round, his 19 Blood lasts 6 rounds.

The section: the stretcher-bearer

Joseph went over with the section, and the GM rules that he is close enough to reach Francis in time. He binds the thigh at Leechcraft 45 and rolls 23: he binds it, taking the bleeding down 2 steps to 1, as in First aid. He cannot carry him back under the guns. Like most of the Newfoundland wounded, Francis lies out in the grass until dark.

The section: the helmet

Near the Danger Tree a shell bursts over Edward. A shell fragment strikes at 70%, with no dodge, and the dice give 31: a margin of 39. Against a fragment the head is serious from 10 and critical from 35, so this is critical.

It strikes his skull, on the left, under his steel helmet. The helmet takes 1 step off a fragment, so the wound is serious. It breaks the bone. It bleeds 2, pain 2, and he is dazed. The stop check: Nerve 50, less 2 steps of pain, gives 30. He rolls 20 and passes: he fights on. Against a bullet the same helmet takes off nothing: it was made for shrapnel.

After dark the stretcher-bearers bring in the men they can find. The wounded go back by motor ambulance, as in After the battle, and onto the track, as in Recovery.

For the GM

The Newfoundlanders were on the field map for about half an hour, and the field map is where they were destroyed: of about 780 who went forward, 68 answered the roll the next morning. Run the exchange for the regiment and the roller for the section, and let the players see how little a good shot or a good stretcher-bearer can do against a machine gun in the open.
